speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture stated that the last census took six years to complete. The census was taken in 1S91 and the general elections were held in 1890, five years afterwards. Was the census not completed when this government came into power?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
There were some of the census staff still in my office and I dismissed them.
Mr. TAYLOR, Were they still doing census work ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: They were working still on census work, as far as I know. They were on the census staff and I suppose they were working at census work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: If the census work was not completed, why were they dismissed ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Because I closed it down.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: If I remember correctly, every volume of the census returns was printed and published one or two years before the election. If it took six years to finish the census, that would bring it down to 1897. That statement can hardly be correct. Now, I will ask the minister where was the work of the 1891 census done ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It was done in the Langevin block-to a large extent; not altogether.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes, the entire census staff was accommodated in the Langevin block, and the Patent branch and the model room were in that building at the same time. When this government came into power they went to their friends and hired a building for the Patent office and the model room, and they left the upper flat of the Langevin block vacant. I ask the minister what takes the place of those departments in the Langevin block now ? How have they managed to fill it up, and to rent buildings from their friends besides. I think the work was completed in 1892 ; but what has been done in these two flats ? Have the departments over there increased the staff so much in four or five years that they hare filled up two flats of the Langevin block with new officials ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: One of the great difficulties I have is to find enough room for the work performed by the different departments. I have been obliged during the last year or two to fit up the attic of the Langevin block for the Indian Department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The Indian Department is in the Eastern block.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Part of it. It also occupies the whole upper

story of the Langevin block. If my bom friend will be kind enough to look over that building, he will And that there is no available room. My hon. friend is a reasonable man, and he knows that the business of this country has increased vastly. For instance, the business of the Department of the Interior has trebled. The business of the Department of Public Works has doubled. He kuows very well that a business man cannot do a business of $500,000 in the same building in which ten years before he was doing a business of only $25,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Is that the difference between the past and the present ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is not quite so much, but it is a vast difference, and that is why we have to have more officials and more room. It is no pleasure to me to rent offices in Ottawa.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It seems to me that there is something in the nature of very bad management in this transaction. The minister says that he made an effort to buy the Seybold property, and got a price on it. He said he was asked $100,000 for the property, and did not take it. The people of Canada would have been better off if he had taken it. The government can borrow money at something under 3 per cent; but he is paying 31 per cent per annum on $100,000

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Only for three years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: And in addition to that he is spending 34 per cent per annum for repairs and charges.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: And furniture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
So that for three years to come he is going to spend 7 per cent on $100,000, twice the amount it would cost the people of Canada if he had bought the property. But, surely it would not be necessary to pay $100,000 for it. The property was sold a short time ago for $20,000, and surely it would have been possible for the government to have taken possession of it under expropriation proceedings. Then it would have been the subject of arbitration, and would probably have been got for $30,000 or $40,000; and, besides, all the improvements made on it would have become the property of the people of Canada. If, as the hon. geutleman says, the government are pressed to find accommodation for the Increased number of public servants who are coming here, it strikes me that he should look a little further ahead, and realize what every member of parliament realizes before lie is here three months, namely, that the accommodation provided for parliament and the public officials is perfectly inadequate. He should not wait until real estate advances
to an extravagant figure. Intelligent management on the part of the Minister of Public Works would have dictated that he should have advised his colleagues to proceed at once to secure such real estate within the neighbourhood of the public buildings as would give the government of Canada accommodation not only for the present but for the future. I should think a scheme which would involve the purchase of the whole block between Metcalfe and O'Connor streets and Wellington and Sparks streets would be a capital investment. The minister would deserve more commendation if, instead of pursuing a piecemeal policy, involving vast expense to the country, he would formulate some proper business-like scheme which would give to parliament and the officials the accommodation they must have, not only for the present, but for years to come.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I am afraid that the same practice obtains in some of the departments as we find about this House. During the last few years, since hon. gentlemen opposite came into office, we find in every portion of this building, both downstairs and upstairs, where rooms were available a few years ago for the use of members, there are none available to-day. What has become of them ? They have been taken for the accommodation of the additional employees engaged by the party for the time being in power, until we find all the rooms practically occupied by a few officials. I presume it is the same in the different departments, and thus we find the government renting buildings here and there and filling them up with the army which they are employing to do the work of the country. I wonder what will be the case when we get through with taking the census. It will be an interesting sight to see what accommodation will have to be provided for that army in the work to be done a few months hence. I think it is time we called a halt. Members of parliament find it difficult to get a seat anywhere around here to do their private work. Rooms which were available a short time ago are not available to-day. They are taken up by the Speaker of the House or the Deputy Speaker or by some employees, and members of parliament who come to do the business of the country are told, You have no interest in these rooms or control over them; they belong to us. They are controlled by the Speaker, or the Sergeant-at-arms, or some other official, and we are denied the use of these rooms-for the business we are called here to do. A few years ago the members of the opposition had seven rooms; but three of them were taken away this year, and were given either to the friends of ministers, or to some employees. We had formerly a large general room downstairs, which was at one time used as a drinking room; but we cannot use it any longer. If a member wants to bring a private secretary here to

(lo any work, he lias no place to go. Sometimes lie is told to go to the library, and the library people tell us, You have no right to bring these people here. And there is no place else to take them. I think that the same thing is going on with regard to other departments. They are being filled up by a large army of employees, friends of hon. gentlemen opposite, whom they are pensioning on the country for many years to come. Hence comes the necessity for renting other buildings and paying very high rents-rents out of all proportion to the value of the buildings. If it is necessary that we should have these buildings, they can he purchased for a very moderate sum. Instead of renting them at the figures we are doing, we should rather buy them and save paying such large rents.
But I am told that we do not need them at all, and I presume, if ordinary economy were exercised, they would not be required. The country has not developed to such an extent in the meantime, and the work of the department has not developed to such an extent that we should require to rent new buildings for the public service.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
In view of the highhanded manner in which the hon. minister acted in the past when he rented the Nagle building, we ought to know what he is doing at present. Iu that case the Minister of Public Works rented a building which was sold for .$(5,000, and after spending $5,000 on it in repairs, he paid a rental of $1,800 per year. It is true that that matter is not under discussion, but in the item before the House the minister is paying $3,500 a year for a building and spending $10,000 on it for repairs, and that building was sold a few years ago for $20,000. Capitalizing the rent paid, that would mean that this building' is to-day worth over $60,000, and yet it was sold at public auction for $20,000.
What are the facts ? A few years ago, when the census was taken and when all the public officials were occupying the present building, there was still ample room for the census staff, and to-day the Minister of Agriculture has rooms rented on Sparks street, to which he has transferred a number of the patent officials and the models, so that there is more room to-day in the Lange-vin block than there was ten years ago. It is nothing short of an outrage to ask us to pay $3,500 a year for the next three years for this building and spend $10,000 in repairing it. and if this vote passes, every bit of repairs done will be done by day labour and not by contract under competition, just as the hon. minister has work done from time to time on other public buildings. The hon. gentleman has been deliciousi.v frank to-day, and the reason we have not far to seek. He has been thwarted in his idea. He never wanted to rent a building, but wanted to build another large departmental block, and now that he has been foiled in that design by his colleagues, the House is Mr. SPROULE.
getting the benefit of his revenge in all these details which he has given.
The MINISTER ' OF AGRICULTURE. The hon. gentleman has re-stated that this building is worth about $20,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I ventured no such opinion, but I said it was sold at public auction for $20,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I would like to know on what occasion that was and how much mortgage was assumed at the time by the purchaser. If the hon. gentleman will undertake to get any valuator in Ottawa to value that building alone, without the land, as it stands, at less than $50,000, I would be very much surprised.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Did the government take any such precaution V

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am not aware that they did. That is a matter which concerns the Public Works Department. The hon. gentleman went on to make other statements which were wider of the mark than many others. He said that the Minister of Agriculture had moved a lot of his staff down to another building in Sparks street with a lot of models. There is not a member of the staff iu that building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Why does the hon. gentleman allow all those beautiful models to be unprotected by his staff ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
There is a caretaker there from the Department of Public Works who keeps that room as he used to do the room in the Langevin block when the models were there. As soon as we get possession of the Seybold building, that room can be given up and the rent saved and we can deduct the rent of that room and the room adjoining, occupied by the Public Works Department, from the rent of the Seybold building.
As to the work in the Langevin block, the hon. gentleman does not understand what occurred after the fire in what is known as our western departmental building. At the time there was a large number of clerks in the public service, accommodated in the attic of the western block. We all know the deplorable loss that we suffered from that fire. We found that the attic was practically a fire-trap and that it would not be proper to allow public records and papers and men engaged in public works to continue in such rooms. The same condition was found to exist in the attic of the eastern block, where a large number of clerks of the Interior DeI ailment were accommodated in a way in which it was a shame that men engaged in the public service should be kept. Valued records of the Interior Department were stored in that attic, and had a fire started it would have been practically impossible to save them. We would lose records that

could not be replaced, valuable interests in the North-west Territories would be injured, and endless litigation would follow. The result was that the Interior Department was moved bodily to the Langevin block. The rooms formerly occupied by the models were placed at the disposal of that department and the rooms oil the floor below. In my own Department of Agriculture, the number of employees has, to a certain extent, increased in consequence of the largely increased work done, and I was obliged to take for that work the rooms formerly occupied by the census staff. To-day in the Langevin block there is no accommodation for the census staff, and consequently the Minister of Public Works has to look about for a building in which to do that work. The Patent Office also has increased in the number of employees, in consequence of the large increase of applications for patents and of an effort on my part to overtake the arrears in the applications for patents which were before the department when we came to office. The Interior Department has also largely increased and requires greater accommodation. The result is that every room and every space for a desk in the Langevin block was occupied before the work of the census began. Until the Seybold building is ready for occupation, it is impossible to carry on the work of preparing for the census except under extreme disadvantage. Hon. gentlemen opposite have talked about the erection of a new departmental building. It is possible that it would be wise to construct such a building. But everybody knows perfectly well that the work of construction would occupy at least two years. Meanwhile, the day for the census is fixed, the work must go on, and the clerks who are to do the work must be accommodated. Therefore, the lion. Minister of Public Works, instead of undertaking the construction of a building, buying a suitable building, as was suggested by my hon. friend from Pictou (Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) rented a building until such time as a decision as to a new public building can be come to. I venture to say that it is not fair to make comparison as between the new work carried on by the customs in the Nagle building or the work of the census, and the Work being done when the present government came into office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Now that the hon. Minister of Agriculture has, I hope to his own satisfaction, shown, first, that a census is going to be taken, and, next, that it is desirable that a census should be taken, let us discuss the question of this building. 1 would like to ask the Minister of Public-Works how it is Intended to expend this $10.000-by his favourite method of day's work or by tender and contract i

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
The money will be spent in buying furniture and in making necessary repairs. And
these repairs, as every one knows who is familiar with these matters, cannot be done otherwise than by day's labour. My hon. friend has just alluded to the western block. He reproached me with having built that by day's labour. I did it that way, and I employed union men, and for that I was congratulated by all the union men in Canada. I say without hesitation that, when you can find good foremen, work carried on by day's labour is cheaper and better than that done by public tender and contract. I am surprised that my hon. friend would even suggest that, for repairs of this kind, tenders should be asked for. There is a partition to be put here, a door to be cut there, and so on. Where is the sensible man who will say that such work can be done by tender and contract ? My hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) says that I am very anxious to erect a new building. I have no anxiety about it ; but it is quite evident that some accommodation must be provided. I know very well that when I shall come and ask for money to put up a new building, I shall be strongly opposed, and accused of wanting to spend money lavishly. But now I am told that because I want to rent a building, I am spending the money foolishly. My hon. friends on the other side are very hard to please. I have not pleased them in the past, and I am afraid I shall not succeed much better in the future. But I rely on this-that the sensible men of the country will not take much stock in the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: In Ontario ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We shall see in a short time whether Ontario will take stock in them or not. Ontario needs only to be talked to a little in order to understand. I have great confidence in Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: But Ontario has not much confidence in the hon. minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. member for Pictou should not speak of a province lacking confidence in me. The hon. gentleman's own province ha:s no confidence in him. He has barely secured his own election. But I have been elected in my own province, and I am here not alone, but some of us are here with a pretty strong backing. Let the hon. gentleman be a little more careful.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: What about Ontario ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Ontario is all right. The hon. gentleman and some of his friends have succeeded in making Ontario wrong. But I am glad to take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. leader of the oppositon (Mr. Borden,

Halifax) of repudiating them. They have appealed to passion and to racial prejudice. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has not done so. I say that sensible men cannot take much stock in the position assumed to-day by hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. member for Bast Simcoe has moved a motion to strike out from the estimates $10,000 that I have agreed to pay to provide means for carrying on the census work of this country. Now, the rental may be a little high. I do not believe it is too high. But, suppose it is, am I going to close the doors of the building upon the staff of the lion. Minister of Agriculture and scatter them to the winds so that no work can be carried on ? My hon. friend has taken an untenable position, and I think if he were a little older and a little wiser, he would not insist upon a vote. I have no more to say except this-that my long experience, both in the press gallery and in this House, leads me to believe that a party does not gain much by such tactics as those of my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) is resorting to.
Mr. TAYLOIt. The hon. Minister of Public Works and the hon. Minister of Agriculture speak as though tnis census work had come up suddenly. These hon. gentlemen have been in power since 1896. They knew that the census was to be taken iu 1901. Why in the world was not some provision made a year of two ago ? Why leave the providing of rooms until the day they want to use them, and then go to a political friend and pay two or three prices for accommodation ? The hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte), a few moments ago, tried to make the House believe that he had gone to every agent and every landlord in the city inquiring for rooms. But when asked to give the names of the parties applied to, he could not give any. This is a case like that of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) stating the other night that every dollar voted-and it is no wonder the opposition protest-is handed out to political friends to pay for goods and services at double prices.
Item voted : Yeas 90, Nays 50.
Slides and Booms-St. Maurice District-
Increased facilities for descent of timber on the St. Maurice river	 $50,000
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC 'WORKS. This sum of money is asked to provide improvements for the descent of timber on the St. Maurice river. These works were begun in 1852, and since that time there has been growing up a magnificent succession of industries, among which I may mention the well known Grande Mere Mills, which this year we expect will consume about 2,000,000 logs. Those works are productive works, that is they yield more than it costs to maintain them. This year we expect to derive a revenue of about $30,000 from these works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: And to spend how much ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
This is only part of the money that will be necessary. The money we will have to spend this year will be over $100,000. These works have cost the country up to date about half a million dollars. In 1899, there was a damaging Hood that carried away a large number of logs, and it is to avoid a recurrence of such an accident that this sum of money is necessary.
Paris Exhibition, $30,000; Buffalo Exhibition, $30,000; total	 $60,000

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: This first item of $30,000 is to close up the accounts in connection with the Paris exhibition. The time has come now when the exhibition accounts can be completely closed up and the work practically completed, provided this money is voted. I may expiain the need of this money by saying that last year I asked an amount that I thought would be necessary for the Paris exhibition, basing my request to the House on a statement which I received from Paris of the expected requirements. I took that request to mean from the date tlxat it was sent to me, but I found afterwards that the commissioners intended it to mean from the 1st of July. Therefore, I made an error of something like $25,000, in the request which I put before the House last session for what I considered necessary to complete the work at the Paris exhibition. A few items have come up since then, amounting to a few thousand dollars beyond what I had expected, and the result is to-day that I am obliged to ask for $30,000 to close the account of the Paris exhibition. I should be glad to give the committee any information they may desire with reference to the Paris exhibition. I will only say just now that from the reports that have been received in this country of the results of that exhibition, the flattering accounts which have come in, not only from all over Canada, but from the press of the world, and from the utterances of a large number of people who visited that exhibition, I feel satisfied that the Canadian exhibit there was worthy of the country, and it has accomplished, in spreading the reputation of Canada as a productive and industrial country, much more than could have been expected from the amount of money there expended I feel extremely gratified at the results of the Paris exhibition, which was conducted unler the management of gentlemen who have shown themselves to be eminently qualified for that work, the whole under the presidency of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: How much has been spent up to date ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I have not at the moment a statement of

the actual expenses up to date, but the total expenditure covered by this vote and all previous votes will he $315,000. Before this I had a vote of $285,000, and this $30,000, making $315,000, I am satisfied from the estimates laid before the department by the commissioner now in charge will cover all the expense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I would like to ask if this is the only detail we are to get concerning this item, a mere request for another $30,000?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am perfectly willing to give all the Information that the committee require. I will give full details of the expenditure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: How much did the commissioner receive for his expenses ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Which commissioner ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Public Works. I suppose he was the one in charge ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The chief commissioner, Hon. Mr. Tavte, received an advance of $3,000 when going to Paris, and $3,000 more was later sent forward, making a total of $6,000 for the commissioner's work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: How long was he away ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: About five months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Did his salary as minister go on while he was acting as commissioner ?
The B1INISTER OF AGRICULTURE. Yes, certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: And he got all these thousands of dollars while his salary was accruing ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: He got no salary as commissioner to Paris.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No, but he got $6,000 all the same.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes, that was placed at his credit.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: How many other commissioners were there ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
There was originally a board of eight commissioners, four being officers of various departments and four being appointed specially to this work. Three of these special commissioners went over to Paris. Prof. Robertson, who is one of the officers, was 30
obliged to make a trip there for a few weeks, Prof. Saunders went there to represent Canada at agricultural conventions, and Mr. Gourdeau, the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, was in Paris the most of the time, I think, all the time from the opening of the exposition. The hon. Minister of Public Works was away from Canada about five months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Are we to be furnished with all the details of the expenditure of these commissioners and the chief commissioner ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The details will appear in the accounts of the commission. I have not them available here now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Are they in the Auditor General's Report ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: They are, up to the 30th June.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That does not cover the interesting part of the accounts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: They will appear in the Auditor General's Report for next year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Then, we will have the pleasure of waiting a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Deferred pleasure ; that is all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We must have the particulars of all the bills that make up this expenditure of $315,000. How much did the building cost ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The building cost $87,600, and we received back $10,600 which we had paid to the Imperial commission for accommodation in the Imperial space. They charged us that, but they returned us the amount I have stated. Our share of the cost of the colonial building, which was to embrace the colonies of the empire, was $76,958, practically $77,000.

speechtext: That was for space ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: For the Canadian share of the colonial building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That is in addition to the $87,000 for the Canadian building ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No, no ; there was no Canadian building. There was a British colonial building, for which we had to pay our share, and our share amounted to the sum of $77,000 in round figures.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
A gentleman who is quite competent to judge, I should say, told



me that he saw the Canadian building at Paris, and he estimated that he could put up that building for $10,000 and make a profit on it at that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am sorry for that gentleman's judgment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I can say to the hon. minister that if he knew that gentleman as he is known in the city of Toronto, he would have a good deal of respect for his judgment. That is his statement about this building. Every statement I have heard is to the same effect, that the moneys which it had been rumoured were paid for that building were exorbitant. We have the statement of a total expenditure of $315,000 and the disbursement of it. The chief commissioner, while drawing his salary as Minister of Public Works in Canada, and performing none of the duties of the Minister of Public Works for all these five months in the year, was drawing $6,000 of our money, and if the newspaper reports were correct, he was spending a large portion of his time in England, where the duties, I presume, of chief commissioner at the Paris Exposition, would not call him. I would like to know if the minister would read to us the details of the whole expenditure so that we may have them before us. We are entitled to that before we vote any more money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Allow me to explain, Sir.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I would like to have the explanation of the hon. Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman have the kindness to hear me ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We will listen to any information that is given.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must do so. The hon. gentleman stated somewhere during the last campaign that I had spent $100,000 in erecting this building, which, he has repeated to-day, could be erected for $10,000. I had nothing whatever to do with this building. When I reached Paris the building was up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Or it never would have been.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The building was up. The hon. Minister of Agriculture had arranged with the Imperial government that Canada would form part of the colonial exhibit. The charge of the building had been entrusted to a Royal Committee in England. Then, I say, when I reached Paris the building was up. I must immediately say that the building was not creditable to us. It was nobody's fault except the fault of the Royal Committee. Not one single member of the committee had crossed the channel and gone to Paris.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I immediately sent for the architect and I asked him where the specifications were. I could not get hold of them, and I only saw them a few days before I left. I asked him whether there were any specifications and whether they had been followed. I took him around the building and he was obliged to admit and recognize that the specifications had not been followed. I asked him whether he had given notice to the Royal Committee, and he said : * No, I did not give notice.' I immediately communicated with my colleague and with Lord Strathcona, and we did with a bad job the best we could. To say that the building is only worth $10,000 is, if I may be permitted without offence to say, stating something which is ridiculous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: How much would you say it would be worth ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I would say between $40,000 and $45,000. I visited the building with one of my colleagues. One of my colleagues was in France and that same gentleman, no doubt that the hon. gentleman alludes to, a big contractor, was with me. Several Canadians came there and admitted that the building was not creditable to us. It proves that at the next exhibition we should go on our own hook. When my colleague went to London all the colonies had undertaken to take part in the exhibition. It came out that only Western Australia and Canada took part in 'the exhibition. Practically we were alone, because Western Australia is a pretty small colony and had only an exhibit of gold. When I reached Paris we could not even get admission to the exhibition grounds without going to the English officers and asking for tickets. My hon. friend (Mr. Wallace) reproaches me with having gone to England. Well, I have gone there and I will go again I hope, and I went there on that occasion in connection with the exhibition. I felt that Canada as the independent nation we are, as a selfgoverning country, was entitled to have a proper standing at Paris. I went to the Royal Committee and represented to them that I would not stay in Paris unless I were credited directly to the French authorities. I did not care for myself. It was easy for me to have a personal standing in Paris, for I have relations there, but I made up my mind that I was doing my duty towards Canada in insisting that Canada should be properly represented. The Royal Committee did not seem to understand me, and then I prepared a memorandum that was forwarded through Lord Strathcona to Mr. Chamberlain, and it is my duty and pleasure and pride to say that forty-eight hours after Mr. Chamberlain read my statement I was directly accredited to the French authorities. I went to England for that very purpose on two occasions. My hon. friend from West York (Mr. Wallace) believes

that I have spent a great deal of money. Well, X have spent $6,000 of the money of the people of this country. Will you permit me to state here that I should have spent a great deal more. Forty-two nations were represented in Paris, and I am sure that I am the commissioner who spent the least ol' all those. There were smaller nations whose commissioners spent a great deal more money than I did. I do not of course compare my position to that of the English commissioner, but I am sure that Col. Jenkin has spent in entertaining and advertising his country a larger sum of money than some hon. gentlemen imagine. Those who have been a minister, those who have travelled; those who know what a nation is; those who know what a great exhibition is, will not reproach me with having spent too much money. Perhaps I may be permitted to say that I have spent a very large sum of money which I have not the means to stand. I judge from reading the debates in the House (I trust that I may say it without offence to anybody), that the position was not stated as it should have been stated. I wrote to some friends of mine on the other side of the House begging them not to make such statements as were made. An ex-minister of the Crown whom I am sorry not to see here stated in the House that we should not have spent more than $25,000 on the Paris exhibition. We have spent about $300,000, and we obtained the grandest advertisement that Canada ever obtained on the European continent. Our exhibit was a most creditable one, and if the building -with which we had nothing to do-was not creditable, the exhibit was most creditable to us, and I must compliment my hon. colleague and friend (Hon. Mr. Fisher) and his officers on the splendid showing they have made on behalf of Canada. I may say that all the staff in Paris did their duty thoroughly and faithfully. As far as I am concerned myself, X have done my best to advertise Canada in France, and in Belgium, and everywhere I was able to speak. If an account of my speeches is asked for at a latter period I shall be most delighted to give it to the House, but we are discussing a financial question just now. I have no hesitation is saying that no expenditure of money will bring to us better results than the money that was spent on the Paris exhibition.

I cannot tell off-hand, but I trust sufficient to make a very creditable display.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I made some remarks in the House last year with reference to the Paris exhibition, and I do not know that we could have a better opportunity than this of getting explanation from the minister on what seemed to me then to be improper conduct on his part. I refer to the reception to President Loubet. The president as the representative of France visited the exhibition, and I presume expected to be received by Col. Jekyll, the representative of the British Empire in his department. That would appear to be proper, but the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) contended that it should take place in the building belonging to Canada, and that as he was there to represent a portion of the British Empire, an independent country, that the reception should take place in the Canada department. If it did not take place there, in a somewhat peevish way the minister declared that he would close the Canadian exhibit. In my judgment such conduct on his part was very improper and some explanation should be made by the minister regarding it. I have no doubt that he will give an explanation that may put a different face on it from that conveyed by the information we got from the press of this country. As to the exhibition itself, I have a letter from a friend who was in Paris, and he does not seem to have quite as high an opinion as to the value of that exhibition as the Minister of Public Works has. He speaks of it in some respects as being creditable, and other respects he thought it was not a fair representation of Canada. He says :
As to the exhibits here, they were not what they ought to have been. I have seen better individual exhibits at provincial fairs in my own country. It was ahead of Australia and perhaps India, hut it could not touch Mexico either for design of the pavilion or beauty of arrangement. It was all right in one thing, that it did not go in_for a foolish display of niclcnacks, to the detriment of industrial exhibits. Compared to the arrangement and character of the Russian exhibit, it was very poor, as outside of the exhibits purely and simply, no information was given regarding the country either as regards colonization or industrial purposes. All Canada wants for success to-day is capital, and there is plenty of it lying idle here awaiting favourable opportunity of investment, but the details of mining and other wealth of the country were altogether too meagre to attract the attention of any capitalists. There was a large amount of space taken up with a lot of trash, such as exercise books for school children of ten or twelve years of age, and you will no doubt know what kind of an exhihit that would be. Such things as this made the exhihit look rather childish, in my judgment. The rest of the ex-

Mbit represented the industries of Canada well enough. Had the arrangements been better, and had more information been given, and also had the materials of which the exhibit consisted been of a higher class, it would have been much better. The art , exhibit was simply ridiculous.
I am not one of those who feel inclined to criticise very severely the amount of money spent by the minister, because while he was there, I am bound to believe that he was trying to do the best he could for his country, and a man in that position cannot be niggardly. Therefore, if there was more spent by him than we might think necessary, we must make allowances. Some of those who visited the exhibition say that it was a comparative failure, while others say that it was a great success. X have given that as the evidence of a Canadian who was living there and going in and out day after day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture how it happened that there was no proper supervision over the construction of this building. I understand from the Minister of Public Works that he regarded the building as unsuitable, as not built according to the specifications, and as worth very much less than we paid for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I will give the hon. gentleman full explanations after recess.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
The MINISTER OF 'PUBLIC WORKS. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has rendered a great service to me in asking me to explain the incident of the visit of President Loubet. One morning I read in the Paris newspapers that the president was going to visit the exhibits of the foreign colonies. I had not been notified, although I had been directly accredited to the French authorities. I made preparations. To understand the matter properly, it is necessary to know that there were three main doors to the colonial pavilion on the Avenue d'lena. In that pavilion Canada had, of course, the largest place. If I remember rightly, Canada had 90 per cent of the space, and paid 90 per cent or thereabouts of the cost. Then, there was Western Australia, and the little island of Mauritius. I made preparations to receive M. Loubet by our main door. In this country, we are in the habit of receiving by our main door, not by our kitchen door. But I found that the British understrappers, who had managed to log-roll in London, had arranged for President Loubet to come in, not by the main door of the building, the Canadian door, but simply by one of the small doors, and only to pass through a small section of Mr. SPROULE.
the Canadian exhibit. He would simply go into our kitchen and see the stove exhibit, and a small corner of the Canadian exhibit. I felt that it was my duty to Canada not to allow British understrappers to slight us in that way; and if any hon. gentleman from the other side of the House had been there representing this country, he would have done just what I did. I am glad to say that there were present, when that incident happened, not only French Canadians, but a large number of English Canadians, and they all sided with me to a man. As I say, preparations had been mads. A band of music had been engaged. There were three or four hundred Canadians of all creeds and races there to receive M. Loubet and the distinguished people who were accompanying him. When I learned that we were going to be slighted in that way, I said to one of those English officers that I would rather close all the doors of the colonial building than submit to such an insult. My hon. friend from Grey is altogether wrong when he is under the impression that M. Loubet's visit was intended for the British pavilion. It was intended for the foreign colonies. The British pavilion was on the Avenue des Nations, on the other side of the Seine, while the colonial, or rather the Canadian building, was on Trocadero square-two different places altogether. Mr. Crozier, chief of the protocol, was informed of the incident, and as soon as he learned that such a trick had been attempted upon the president, he changed all the arrangements on the spot, and the president came into our exhibition by our main door. An explanation was given a couple of days afterwards to the English newspaper men who were in Paris, and I may say that they all congratulated me on the firm stand I took. Now, my hon. friend from Grey is altogether wrongly informed when he states that the exhibition was not a credit to us. As a commercial exhibition, I make bold to say that it was the most complete on the ground. There were European nations which had bigger exhibitions, which had art exhibitions ; but, as a commercial exhibition, the Canadian one was a very great success indeed. The number of prizes or medals it secured is the best evidence of that fact. The exhibition of grain, of lumber, of minerals and of fruit was very fine. I do not know that I need say anything more, except to add that the Canadian commissioners and staff at Paris did their duty faithfully towards this country. We had a little trouble and a great deal of work. As has been truly said, the building was not what it should have been, and we were obliged to spend some money in decorating it, but when we had covered our sheds with drapery and other decorations, it looked very presentable.
I must take strong exception to what has been said by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) concerning the educa-

tional exhibit. Our educational exhibit was a great credit to us. The province of Ontario, perhaps, did not do as well as she should have done, but all the other provinces had very nice exhibits, and I think the installation of our educational exhibit was one of the best, if not the best, in the building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
That only shows the different impression created on different minds. We have the view of the hon. gentleman who was there to superintend, and who naturally would give as favourable a report as possible, but I have simply given the view of an independent Canadian who went over the exhibit.
I brought to the attention of the House to-night this matter of the reception of President Loubet, because, as represented to us by the press, it certainly bore a very different appearance from what the hon. minister has given us to-night. I brought it to the hon. gentleman's attention for two reasons- not because I was uninformed with regard to it, because I read a lengthy explanation of the hon. gentleman, which satisfied me in a measure that he was perhaps not as much to blame as represented. But my principal object was to give the hon. gentleman an opportunity of giving the House an explanation which would remove the impression in the public mind created by the accounts in the press. As we understood the reports then, it was the duty of Dr. Jekyll, who was the representative of the Imperial parliament, to receive President Loubet, but the hon. minister told us differently, and I am not going to say that there was not good reason for his conduct. But it did seem somewhat out of keeping with the dignity of the situation and what might be expected from a minister of the Crown in a British colony, to use the representative of the British Empire in that way. The hon. gentleman spoke of Dr. Jekyll as the British understrapper.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
No, I never mentioned Col. Jekyll's name-far from it-I am glad to say that he behaved towards us very nicely indeed, but he came very late, and there were other people before he came to whom I could not pay the same compliment. Col. Jekyll behaved towards us like a gentleman and a friend, and on the very occasion of President Loubet's visit he was by my side and was very glad to be with us. But he came to Paris about the same time as I did myself, and the wrong that had been committed towards us was then done. If the commissioners who had been before in Paris, were on the floor of this parliament, without any distinction of origin or creed, they would tell stories that would induce the press on both sides to make up their minds that when Canada again took part in any exhibition anywhere, we should go on our own hook. And I may add that the commissioners at
the Paris exhibition in 1878 told me the same story. We were simply looked down upon and treated, not as representing a selfgoverning nation, but to a certain extent as inferiors. Within my hearing is one of the commissioners, and if he were free to speak he would say something that would astonish you more than anything I have said.
I exonerate completely Col. Jekyll from any blame. When he came to Paris he did his best to help us, and did help us very materially indeed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I came to the conclusion I did from the speech of the hon. gentleman when he said the British understrapper did so and so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Understrappers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I understood the difficulty was with the representative of the British Empire through whom officially any arrangement should be made. I am glad the hon. minister made the explanation because his remarks seemed to reflect in an unkindly manner on the representative of the British Empire. As to the wisdom or otherwise of our taking part in an exhibition of that nature, independent entirely of the British Empire, I am not going to criticise, because I am not in a position to judge. But it seems to me that as long as we are a colonial dependency of the British Empire, it would not be inappropriate if we were in some way or other under the wing of the empire to which we belong, when making a display in a great country like France.
I have given the impression of a Canadian who visited the exhibition. "Where he thought it was defective was largely in the fact that although we had exhibits of our mines, there was, comparatively speaking, no information to be had with regard to our mining laws and the condition of things in this country. In many departments he said the exhibition was a success. He spoke of our fruits being very fine and serials, but that, in his judgment, in some other lines it was very poor, and he spoke especially of the exhibit of educational books for children and the art department as being very poor. I am not giving my own Impression but only those of one who went there on a visit.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I do not mean to say that Canada should be altogether independent of England. I did not mean anything of the kind. But we are a self-governing colony, we are making our own tariff, for instance, quite independent of England. An exhibition is a question of business and not of foreign policy, just as when we are making our own laws. And in that Paris exhibition, our interests in some lines conflicted with those of British exhibitors. We were large exhibitors in agricultural implements, and so was England. We were large exhibitors in cotton,

and so was England. Before I reached Parisian arrangement had been made that sixty judges altogether would be given for the British Empire, including her colonies. We were occupying 44,000 feet of the ground in the British Empire, and the British Empire itself was occupying 200,000 feet, so that we were entitled to have about one-fifth of the judges in number. I found that we had only four. I said that that was wrong and insisted strenuously ou being given more.
Arrangements were made. It was agreed between the English and the French authorities, as I say, that sixty judges should be given for the whole British Empire. Of that number, the British Commission in London had given only four judges to Canada. Was that reasonable, was that fair, especially when we had interests conflicting with those of the British exhibitor ? In questions of business the Englishman does not care much whether you are an English Canadian or a French Canadian-if he has to fight against you he does it ; if he can carry the medals and prizes against you he does it. I insisted strongly on a change, and, with the help of-Lord Strathcona and Mr. Chamberlain, I gained some small points. The correspondence asked for by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) will show the strenuous efforts wie made to secure, not justice, but a small share of justice. We did not get the number of judges we should have got. But the thing turned out right.
I represented to Colonel Jekyl that if the Canadians did not get the prizes to which they were entitled, there would be great disappointment and resentment in Canada. He helped me to the best of his ability. I give these explanations at some length because I feel that this is not a party question. There will be other exhibitions. My hon. friends opposite may then have crossed the floor. If so, they will find themselves sometime in the same position that we were In ; and I beg of them, as I beg of my friends on this side, to take the stand, once for all, that we are a self-governing country; and, in matters of business let us stand by Canada-Canada before all. That does not prevent us from being good, loyal subjects of the King. But we have business of our own, we have a realm of our own, and let us try to exploit it to the best of our ability.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I have been much pleased to find that, at the Paris exposition the province of Prince Edward Island was among the foremost in taking prizes. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that for oysters, one of the products of Prince Edward Island, we were awarded first prize. Those who love to partake of the luscious bivalve will be pleased to know that at that great exhibition. where the province was brought into competition with the whole world, it won first prize. But we have in Prince Edward Island other products besides oysters. We Mr. TARTE.
produced there an individual who was elected to the legislature a little over a year ago to oppose the local government. His name is Pineau. He was a Conservative and was elected by the Conservative people of Prince county. The local government was in extremis, and if Mr. Pineau got in, it was believed they would have to resign. But what do we find ? The Minister of Public Works states that he was in need of help in Paris. If he had taken Mr. Pineau with him he would have had all the help he required. Mr. Pineau was approached by an agent of the government, Dr. Wickham, in Tignisli, the district in which he was elected. This gentleman went to Mr. Pineau and said : If you will support the local government, or if you will leave the province and go to Paris as commissioner of the Dominion government you will be paid a salary of $5 a day and $5 a day expenses. Mr. Pineau came to Ottawa. Would not you consider it a singular proceeding for a man elected by the independent people of Prince county to oppose the party to which the hon. Minister of Public Works belonged should come here and remain for a week in the very shadow of this building in conference with the hon. gentleman or his agents ? He was. purchased by the government, and that fact remains a stain, a blot, upon our history. But Mr. Pineau did not take the trip to Paris, Mr. Wise, a member of the local legislature upon whom the party of hon. gentlemen opposite were depending for support, opposed the local government, and it was found that the presence of Mr. Pineau in the legislature was necessary and it was-

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I never saw the man.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: He was here for a week, and I am told on the best authority that he was in close communication with the hon. gentleman's (Hon. Mr. Tarte's) private secretary. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) will say that he never saw him. Perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) will say that he never saw him. But the -fact is that Mr. Pineau was waiting here in Ottawa for instructions to go to Paris under the Minister of Public Works. This, I say, is a blot upon our history. When the electors vote for a man, they wish to have him as their representative and not to have him bribed by a hostile government needing his support. While I am proud of one product of Prince Edward Island, the oyster, I am ashamed of the product of Pineau, and I am especially ashamed that I supported the man who came here and sold his support to the Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I am sorry the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) hais given us such a picture of his own province. I confess it is new to me, because

I did not suppose that Prince Edward Island put forth such a product as he speaks of.
I was quite prepared to hear that that province had taken the prize in oysters, because I had the pleasure on many occasions of partaking of those oysters. But, as to the other, the hon. gentleman has surely jumped at a conclusion. I dare say Mr. Pineau was here, but I do not know it. So far as I know, no member of the government saw him here. The hon. gentleman's (Mr. Hac-kett's) friends may have seen him. As minister in charge of the Paris exposition, 1 can tell the hon. gentleman and the House and Prince Edward Island, and the country at large that I never saw Mr. Pineau, never had any communication with him directly or indirectly ; Mr. Pineau did not go to Paris in connection with the Paris exposition, and the hon. gentleman will search in vain in the accounts of the Paris exposition for one cent paid in any way to Mr. Pineau. I trust that this statement is sufficiently categorical to convince the hon. gentleman that, whatever the Conservative electors in Prince Edward Island may choose, they do not choose a man that this government tries to buy or buys in any shape or way. One or two questions were asked me before recess, to which I take great pleasure in replying. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax! asked for explanations in connection with the building in Paris. That building was entirely managed by the Imperial Commission, and the Canadian Commission had neither part nor lot in the contract for its construction of any connection with it.
When the invitation to Canada came to us to participate in the Paris exhibition, it came through the Imperial authorities, as was natural that it should, coming from a foreign country. We were informed that they would be pleased if we would take part as a colony of Great Britain, and that they would make the arrangements necessary to secure a proper opportunity for the various British colonies to be represented at Paris. Those communications indicated to us the steps which the Imperial commission had taken for this object. They informed us that the building would be prepared under their control and management for the products of the colony, and that that building would have to be submitted to the French authorities for acceptance. They asked us if we would take part in an exhibition in that building, and if we would pay our proportion of the cost pro rata to the space occupied. As the minister in charge of these things, after consultation with my colleagues^ and discussion with gentlemen in Canada who had taken some part in former exhibitions. that was agreed to. Lord Strath-cona. the High Commissioner of Canada in London, was appointed as our representative on the colonial committee of the Imperial commission, and all the work in connection with the Imperial commission was
done through Lord Strathcona. Plans of that building came out here, the estimates having been prepared in London, and we were informed that that was what had been arranged for us, and we had either to accept that or refuse to take part in the exhibition.
It happened that summer that I was in England on other business, and I attended one or two meetings of the colonial committee with Lord Strathcona. I made some suggestion in regard to the details and plan of the building, which were taken into consideration and some of them accepted. But on the general question of the plans of that building, its construction, its cost and everything connected with its management, we had practically no word to say. At that time it was expected and intended that Cape Colony, with the various Australian colonies and New Zealand, would take part in the exhibition. We were informed that one-third of the whole space of that building would be at our disposal. We protested energetically that that was not sufficient to a proper representation of Canada at such a great exhibition as that in Paris. From time to time various of the Australian and Crown colonies decided they would not take part, and as they so decided we were asked if we would take the space which had been accorded to them. Finally, the result came about that we had over eighty per cent of the space in that building accorded to us. We took this, not because we desired to do so, but because we found that the Canadian exhibitors, commercial men, manufacturers, agriculturists, men engaged in forest industries, and the lumber trade of this country, were demanding more space than we had at our disposal ; and therefore, we felt it was necessary to have larger space than was at first accorded to us. We, therefore, took the opportunities that were presented to us, and whenever the Imperial authorities informed us that more space was available, we seized upon it greedily in order to satisfy the claims and demands of the Canadian exhibitors who wished to exhibit at Paris.
Hon. gentlemen, therefore, will see that so far as we were concerned, so far as my own management of the department was concerned, so far as the management of our commercial interests was concerned, we had practically nothing whatever to do with the construction or the cost of that building. I may say that when one of the commissioners first went over to Paris and saw the building. he protested against its method of construction, and against the quality of the building. Afterwards, when my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, went over there, he again protested to the Imperial commissioners as to the quality of the building. I am satisfied from what I know, and from the reports given to me since, that that building was not up to the mark, that it was not worth the price that was paid for it ; and I withheld for a long time the final payment, because I believed Canada was

not fairly charged with the amount which the Imperial commissioners asked from us. But after the Minister of Public Works reached Paris and had discussed these questions with Mr. Jekyll and other Imperial commissioners, and with Sir Montague Ommany, Under Secretary for the Colonies, who came over to Paris to look into this matter, and after the Minister of Public Works had gone to London and consulted with Lord Strathcona, the chairman of the colonial committee of the Imperial commission, and after this whole question had been thoroughly discussed, we received a letter from the Imperial authorities stating that as the architect had signed the reports upon the building and had accepted the building, as the contractor had the certificates of the architect for the building and for its construction, we practically had no recourse ; the Imperial authorities distinctly informed us that we had no recourse, and they called upon us to foot the bill. I may say that so far as I saw, we had no recourse. I protested to Lord Strathcona, and asked him to protest to the Imperial authorities in his capacity as chairman of the colonial committee. He did so, and I have in my department to-day a letter from Lord Strathcona, in which he strongly urged me, and advised me, in his capacity as a member of the Imperial commission, and as representing Canada on that commission, to pay the bill and settle the matter, because he could see that we had no recourse, and no other alternative.
That is the position of affairs to-day. I regret extremely to have to say that that building was not commensurate with the demands of Canada for the products which were put into it, and I have no doubt whatever that the inferior character of the building militated considerably against the success of our exhibition there. But when my hon. friend and colleague, the Minister of Public Works, went over to Paris, seeing the inferior quality of the building, seeing there was danger that our exhibits would not be properly presented, and would not look well in that building, he undertook to make some decorations in the interior of the building, and he so far succeeded, with the co-operation of the other commissioners and of our staff there, as to make the building inside a creditable one, and fit for the splendid exhibit which the people of Canada put into it. This added somewhat unexpectedly, but reasonably, I think, to the cost we were put to in regard to this exhibition. I do not think that I need say any more in regard to the building.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Before the hon. gentleman leaves that question, would he say upon whom the duty devolved to look after the character of the building ? In other words, whose duty was it to see that a suitable building should be provided for Canada, for Mr. FISHER.	1
which we had to pay a certain portion of the cost ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The colonial committee of the Imperial commission. on which our representative was Lord Strathcona.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I understand there were specifications sent out here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Plans, but no specifications.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Well, if Canada was going to pay a proportion of the cost of this building, why did not the hon. gentleman see that specifications were produced, so that we might know what we were going to pay for. I would also like to ask the hon. gentleman whether, when it was suggested that we should pay a portion of the cost of this building, any estimate was furnished to him as to what the building would cost ? I am not prepared at present to concur in the view that there should be no recourse. I cannot understand how this business has been transacted so that we pay double what this building is worth, and have no recourse against any one. There must be fault somewhere, and I want to find out where it is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I may say that the whole question lay in the hands of the Imperial commission. We were invited to take part in the exhibition by the Imperial commission. We did not stand as an independent country ; we had to deal with the Parisian authorities through the Imperial commission. When we were invited to attend the Paris exhibition, a request was made that we should deal with the Parisian authorities. That was refused by them and refused by the Imperial authorities, who desired that the British Empire should stand together and act as one empire in connection with the Paris exhibition. The Imperial commission appointed a special committee known as the colonial committee, to deal with colonial exhibits. These were the conditions upon which we should take part in the exhibition. We had to accept or reject them. We might have said that we did not wish to make an exhibit at the Paris exhibition. An estimate was made of the cost in regard to the building. The first letter I had said that it would not exceed 10s. per square foot, and that the cost of administration would not exceed 5s. per square foot. Later on it cost more, and before the final acceptance of the contract the price was stated at 12s. 6d. per square foot. As a matter of fact, the final cost went a little over that even. I can assure the hon. gentleman that in this matter the whole affair was in the hands of the Imperial committee, that we had practically no control, except that we had the right to refuse to go to Paris at all, and the idea we had at

the time the Imperial committee undertook this was that we could safely and satisfactorily entrust to such a committee, composed of the leading men of the empire and representatives of the colonies, whose chairman was Lord Strathcona, the construction and management of such a building, and that our interests would be carefully safeguarded. When that was agreed to and when we accepted that position, we were satisfied that the colonial building was to be for the whole of the British colonies and that we would have about one-third of the space in it, and be obliged to pay only for one-third of the cost. As time went on we accepted further responsibility by taking more space. We were driven to that by the demands of intending exhibitors who desired to show Canadian products in the building, and a refusal to accept their products would have entailed an enormous amount of disappointment to the people who wished to make these exhibits and great loss would have resulted to the Dominion of Canada had not these exhibits gone to Paris. Under these circumstances I cannot see, myself, as the minister in charge of this department, how the government of Canada was in any way responsible for that building. We had to take our share of it as it was given to us by the Imperial commission, and the Imperial commission did all the work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is not at all the question of the empire standing together, so far as I understand it; it is a question of the administration of the hon. gentleman's department. The hon. Minister of Public Works very plainly stated to us, only five minutes ago, that matters of this kind are matters of business.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: They are, I think. Are they not ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: They are matters of business. I agree with the hon. gentleman, and I am quoting him as against his colleague, who seems to think that it is not a matter of business but a matter of keeping the empire together.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Not a bit of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman's explanation is satisfactory. He seems to think that this was a trifling matter because it involved only one-third of the cost of the building, but it is a very considerable sum of money- $25,000 or $30,000. What I venture to suggest is that it would have been a proper thing for him to have proper specifications and an estimate made as a business matter for the purpose of finding out what kind of a building we were going to pay for and how much we were going to pay for it

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We had that information, and if the building had been up to the contract and specifications there would have been no fault found.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Very good ; then, I do not understand how the hon. gentleman expects the committee to believe that there is no recourse. Here are the contractors and here is the architect, here are the specifications and you would expect the architect to proceed according to these. There is the contract to do certain work up to a certain standard and for a certain sum of money. We have the safeguard of responsible contractor's and the safeguard of an architect. Some one must be responsible for seeing that the building would be erected in accordance with the specifications. Either the contractors are liable, or if the contractors have been relieved by any unjustifiable action of the architect, the architect is liable, and I suppose he is a responsible man. How then could the hon. gentleman expect us to understand that there is no recourse against any one ? I do not understand it. If the Imperial commission was the body that dealt with these contractors, have they not a valid claim against the contractors V

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I do not say they have not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has said that there is no recourse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I say that we have no recourse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We have recourse directly or indirectly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We may have recourse against the Imperial commission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I would like to know if the hon. gentleman has asked the Imperial commission or the Imperial government to take action against the contractors ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Through Lord Strathcona, yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: If so, has any action been taken ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: They declined to do so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Well, it would be extremely satisfactory to the committee to have their reply placed upon the Table of the House, so that we could understand it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I have Lord Strathcona's letter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
It would be satisfactory to know why it is that when
the commission made a satisfactory contract with certain contractors to do a certain work, and when that work was super-

vised by an architect, that the work d,one is not up to the value which it should have been, according to the kon. Minister of Public Works, by about one-half? Why is it that, under such idircumstances, the Imperial commission should decline to take action against the contractors V It seems to me that the hon. gentleman should give us some better explanation than merely stating that he has asked them to do this and that they have declined to do it. For what reason have they not taken action against these people, if the facts are as the hon. gentleman states them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Speaking from memory, I may say that the letter in which Lord Strathcona communicates this decision, stated that the Imperial committee found that the architect whom they had employed had given his certificate to the contractors, and that consequently they did not feel that they had any recourse against the contractors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: But, they have recourse against the architect if he is found to have acted improperly. Under t'he circumstances disclosed to this committee hy the hon. Minister of Public Woi'ks, 1 venture to think that they would have a perfect recourse against the architect. 1 would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) wihat is the meaning of the item which i find in the Auditor General's Report, page D-12, and which states that the government has paid this architect-I do not know whether this architect had anything to do with this building or mot-

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
No.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)-three hundred and sixty dollars on account of fees, and $30.12 for a trip to Baden, Switzerland.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That is not the same architect.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: What architect is this ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I will explain that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is another matter altogether.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We will deal with that presently in order that we may close this matter first.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Very well.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
If the architect passed this building, which the hon. Minister of Public Works says is worth only half the money which it cost, he must be liable for his dereliction of duty in doing that, and if the contractors are not liable the architect is. If we cannot have recourse against one we must have recourse against Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
the other, because it is not possible that the money of this country shall be paid out for a default of that kind and no ome be responsible for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
