speechtext: As to this architect, I may explain that when I reached Paris the inside of the building looked like a barn. I thought it was my duty towards the exhibitors and towards Canada to give the building a better appearance, and with the consent of my co-commissioners we engaged a young Canadian, who has been studying in Paris during the last five or six years, and he rendered us very valuable services, and we paid him that sum of money and something more.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Then this vote is for the purpose of assisting to hide the shame ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes. If the bon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) had been there he would have done just as I did.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I have no doubt

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: He would have done better, perhaps, but he would have proceeded on the same lines. As soon as I reached Paris I protested to the Royal Committee in the strongest terms, and that correspondence will be brought down. I represented to them that this Canadian building could not possibly be according to the specifications, but I could not get hold of these specifications until a couple of weeks before I left. No member of the Royal Committee had visited Paris, and the architect, who was the architect of all the other colonial buildings, was left to carry out the work alone.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Does the hon. minister know his name ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
It was Mr. Clowes. I do not see what more could be done by us to protect Canadian interests. The architect had given his certificate, but it was actually raining in the building. I was afraid it would fall on our heads, and we made them strengthen it, and we succeeded at least in preventing the rain from destroying the exhibits. To achieve even that required a good deal of energy. The Canadian government is not to blame in this matter, except that from the start we should have made up our minds to erect our own buildings. The Minister of Agriculture has stated that the French authorities declined to deal with Canada. I am bound to say that on that point my hon. colleague lias not been rightly informed. This is not a party or a government question, and as I have been there I know what took place. The French authorities allowed nations who are less independent commercially than we are, to exhibit on their own hook. Egypt exhibited on her

own liook, and Egypt is not quite as independent as we are. Bulgaria, which is under the thumb of Russia, had an exhibit of her own. If the French authorities alone were concerned we would have been allowed to exhibit as a self-governing nation, because the French authorities realize, as we realize ourselves, that we are a self-governing people. However, I can quite understand the strong desire of the British authorities that the whole empire should stand together at the Paris exposition, and it is to that desire that the Canadian government yielded. Whether we have been right or wrong it is for the Canadian people to judge. Speaking from the experience I acquired in Paris, I say without hesitation that we made a mistake. We meant well, but it would have been better for the British Empire had we exhibited independently as a self-governing colony. We would have been under the wing of the British Empire just as well, but we would have had more prestige ; we would have had more latitude ; we would have had a better social standing, if I may say so. The word ' colony' is not understood on the continent of Europe as it is understood in the British Empire. The word 'colony' in Europe means a subordinate body. As a matter of fact, I do not know that any country other than England has under her wing a single self-governing colony. I had to explain over and over again, every time I had an opportunity of speaking, that we were a self-governing country, because we are not as well known on the other side as some of our friends think we are. It is for these reasons that, perhaps, we have made a mistake, a well-meant mistake, in not exhibiting on our own account as a self-governing country. I cannot repeat too often that an exhibition is a question of business and that there are no foreign relations involved in it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No one pretends for a moment that there is the slightest objection to erecting this building in connection with the other colonies or with the Imperial government. That is not the question. We are delighted to join with the other colonies and with the British government in the erection of the building, but the point is that in doing that we should use ordinary business methods. We should have had estimates and specifications, and, if we find the building has cost more than it is worth, as the Minister of Public Works states

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That cannot be denied.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
In that case we Should be in a position to seek recourse against the person responsible. That is the only point there is about it. All I desire to ascertain is, that the Department of Agriculture, which has charge of that duty, has taken the necessary means towards that
end. I do not think the Minister of Agriculture would venture to deny that some one must be responsible for damages on account of this default. If an architect leaves a building as described by the Minister of Public Works, with the rain coming through the roof, he must be responsible. I do not know whether the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) himself indulged in this pastime with his subordinates, of bailing out the water with buckets and covering up the exhibits when it rained

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That had to be done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Agriculture desires the House to believe that an architect who is guilty of leaving a building in that condition is not to be responsible to any person for his default.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman seems to suggest that there is some hesitation on the part of the commission to have recourse against this architect. I cannot believe that that commission would have any hesitation about proceeding against that architect unless there is some reason that has not yet been disclosed to this House. The hon. gentleman having referred to the letter from Lord Stratheona. I was anxious that he should lay that letter on the Table in order that the House might judge as to the reasons which have been advanced for this course, which seems to me somewhat singular.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am sure that the leader of the opposition has not the slightest desire to misrepresent me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I had no desire to say that nobody had recourse against this architect. What I did say was that he had no recourse against the architect. The Dominion of Canada had no buildings erected there. We were a part of the British Empire invited by the Imperial Commission to take part in that exhibition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: What I understood the hon. minister to say was that Lord Stratheona said there was no recourse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
What Lord Stratheona said was that the Imperial committee were not in a position to take action aainst the contractors, because they had the certificate of the architect. No doubt the hon. gentleman would say that the Imperial committee should take action against the architect. I presume he is right as a lawyer to say so. So far as I know, the Imperial committee did not take any such action, but they did require from me the payment of our share of the

cost of the building. I have the letter, which I shall be only too glad to lay on the Table for the information of the hon. gentleman, because I am sure he will understand that I am not wishing to misrepresent the facts at all; but I do not wish it to go abroad that I am giving the opinion that the Imperial committee had no recourse 'against either the contractor or the architect. What I say is that the Dominion government had no recourse except to pay for our share of the building, which was the condition on which we accepted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I would like to ask at what stage had the building arrived when the Canadian commissioner first protested ? Also, at what stage had the building arrived when the Minister of Public Works raised a protest. I understood from the Minister of Agriculture that protests had been raised on two different occasions by the two gentlemen to whom I have referred.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
The first protest I think was verbal on the part of one of the commissioners, who saw the Imperial agents on the subject. I could not tell the hon. gentleman at what stage the building had arrived. It was a few weeks or perhaps a month before the opening of the exhibition. The Minister of Public Works did not reach Paris until just before the opening of the exhibition.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). The building was then completed 7

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Nearly completed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I reached Paris on the 117th of March, and, if I remember rightly, I went to the building the very day after I arrived. I had with me Mr. Clowes and Mr. Humphrey, one of the contractors, and I told them at once that, although I was not an expert, I had enough experience to be sure that no architect would specify such a building; and I protested immediately afterwards to Lord Strathcona. We several times obliged Messrs. Humphrey & Company to improve the building, and make it as good as it was possible to make it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is a good thing that this House and this country are not often treated to the spectacle which we have here to-night-two ministers acknowledging to the grossest negligence and incapacity in the management of their departments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Nothing of the kind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: They shake their heads. What was the speech of the Minister of Public Works ? Was it not confession from beginning to end that everything had gone wrong ? Our money was voted by the parliament of Canada two years ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture came here and asked parliament for $175,000 for the Paris exposition. That was after careful estimates and calculations of the space that would be required, and he pledged himself to the House and the country that nothing would be left undone to see that the money was carefully and economically expended, that good value would be obtained for it, and that competent men would be got to administer it. What do we find to-day ? $140,000 is required in addition to the $175,000, which we were assured would be all that would be required; $140,000, and more than that absolutely thrown away without any beneficial results for the people of Canada. It is a confession of incompetence from start to finish. \\ nat did the Minister of Public Works tell us a moment ago? He admitted that all was wrong, but he said the Canadian government were not to blame. He has a habit, which we have seen a hundred times in this House, if anything goes right, to claim credit for the genius and the admirable management of the Minister of Public Works, whereas if anything goes wrong, he says, It is my staff-I will cut their heads off. I think we have had enough of that sort of thing. He told us that in his opinion the building was worth $40,000 or $50,000. I do not know where he got the experience to be a competent judge. For myself, with the greatest deference to him, I refuse to acknowledge his judgment in the matter at all, especially as his interests 'all go to make the value of the building as great as possible. A gentleman in Toronto, capable and competent, said he could put up that building for $10,000, and I will take his opinion a hundred times over on that matter before the opinion of the Minister of Public Works. The hon. gentleman says the Canadian government are not to blame. Who is to blame ? We voted the money, and the Minister of Agriculture gave us the assurance that it would be economically, carefully, and wisely expended. He told us of his plans and schemes. Where are those plans and schemes to-day ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: All carried out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: All scattered to the four winds of heaven-nothing carried out. Like all the plans and schemes which the Minister of Agriculture has presented to the House in times past, they have been an utter failure. Now, I am a little mystified about this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite say ' hear, hear.' They are mystified also. First, one minister went over, then another, then a whole army of ministers crossed the Atlantic, and visited Paris, and took in the exhibition, and viewed the buildings, and enjoyed themselves, all at

the public expense. I say we are mystified, and the ministers themselves are unable to give the particulars. To get out of it, they say this is not a party question. What is it ? The party on this side of the House had nothing to do with the expenditure of these thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars. AM we did was to vote the money, and we did it with fear and trembling, because we knew it would not be put to a good and proper use; and our fears have been verified. Why, I read in the Auditor General's Report this item ; Payments to Colonial commission on account of space, &c., $87,600. This is only on account. Is that for the building that was erected jointly by the Canadian and by the other British governments ? I would like to ask that question of the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Public Works, or anybody that happens to know it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That was for the Royal commission, for the building and the space in the Imperial space in the main building, both included. Out of that we received back $10,641 from the Imperial commission as they had made a mistake in charging us for space included in their own allotment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am delighted to know that we got $10,000 back. But this is only a payment on account and we have no information as to the total amount. Is this the total ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
It is satisfactory to find that we paid only $87,000 for nothing and got back $10,000 of it.
There is another item here. I see that one H. Pabre had appartments fixed up for him, I presume in this building. Is that correct ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Where ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
In
the city of Paris, rue Jerome.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Then the government of this country, without an appropriation from parliament for that purpose-

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: There was nothing said, when the government asked the vote of $175,000, about $7,641 being paid to fix up the appartments of Mr. Pabre in the city of Paris. Why should that be charged against the Paris exhibition ? This was not in the exhibition at all but miles away in the city of Paris. It was the residence of Mr. Hector Pabre. The minister has told us so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I did not tell you anything of the kind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Did the bon. gentleman not say it was in the city of Paris ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes, but I did not say it was the residence of Mr. Pabre.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: What residence was it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
It
was the offices and not the residences.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I must say that the offices are delightful and beautiful to behold-something that would charm the eye and please all the senses. In the office there is an ante chamber and to furnish that chamber with Wilton carpets and chairs- two at $27 each-and a letter box $19.30, and a lot of other things, cost $186. Then there is the reading room, laid also with Wilton carpets at an expense of $99.97, a table $57.90, book-case $86.85, desk $13.50, two arm chairs $57.90, six other ordinary common chairs $81.06. The total for the reading room is $419.75. This is just a common every day office.
Then you come to the rotunda and veranda: Wilton carpet $52.83 ; curtains and poles $26.63; window blinds, $26.05; table, $28.95; three chairs, $40.54 ; large sofa, $86.85 ; three easy chairs, $86.85, and sundry other things on the rotunda and veranda, making a total of only $367.42.
Then we come to room No. 1 and there we find a Wilton rug, $19.30 ; curtains and other hangings, $19.30 ; window blinds, $10.62, one sofa, $28.95 and one $19.30 ; easy chair, $18.34 ; two office chairs, $13.52 ; walnut cabinet, $11.58 ; office table, $19.30, and so on, and that room only cost $203.63.
These are the poorly furnished shed offices of Mr. Fabre in Paris. Then we come to room No. 2: Wilton carpet, $66.17; two sets window hangings, $48.25 ; two pairs curtains, $5.79 ; blinds, $11.58 ; mantel decoration, $4.83; sofa, $57.90; office chair, $15.44 ; two easy chairs, $57.90 ; two chairs, $27.02 ; desk, $96.50 and wardrobe, $33.81. This room only cost $424. This is one of the commoner rooms apparently required for offices in the city of Paris. I would like to know what return we get for the moneys spent.
Then we come to room No. 3 : Wilton carpet, $56.62; window hangings, $19.30; blinds, $4.83 ; mantel decorations, $4.83 ; desk, $19.30 ; book-case, $31.84 ; office chairs, $12.55 ; sofa, $48.25 ; easy chair, $27.02 ; two chairs, $27.02. Total for that room only $254.45.	.
Then we come to room No. 4, and I think that when the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Agriculture were around they must have been entertained in room No. 4 :	Wilton carpet, $93.23 ; two sets
window hangings, $61.76; two pairs curtains, $5.79 ; blinds, $9.65 ; four double portieres, $115.80 ; mantel ornaments, $4.83 ; table, $11.58 ; desk, $96.50 ; book-case, $67.55 ;

table, $19.30 ; office chair, $14.48 ; two chairs, $27.02 ; drawing-room furniture one set : Sofa, two easy chairs and four 'Other chairs, $347.40-making a total for the drawing-room of only $874.89.
Then we come to room No. 5 : Wilton carpet, $54.43 ; window hangings, $19.30 ; blinds, $4.83-a good many blinds-

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Pull down the blinds.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I suppose that is what the hon. minister would like-to pull down the veil of oblivion over all these entertaining items. Mantel decorations, $4.83 ; one blind, $7.72; desk, $96.50; mahogany, $38.60; office chair, $14.47-in all, $388.32.
Room No. 6 and other rooms follow and a number of other items. And in addition to all the items 1 have read, and deducting $1,300 or $1,400 for Insurance, and so on, we still have $3,000 and more for furnishings in addition to the items 1 have read.
Where did they put the $3,000 additional furniture ? Under what authority did they act ? When did parliament give them power to make these expenditures ? Was this expenditure part of the programme the Minister of Agriculture had in mind when he asked us for $175,000, and told us what he was going to do to make an exhibit worthy of the Dominion ? Now we find the money squandered, we find that the ministers have helped themselves liberally, and no account given, of course. They say : You cannot entertain in <i way to show Canada off in the best light without spending money. Why, Mr. Chairman, when we looked at the newspapers of that time; we saw telegrams : ' Mr. Tarte is in London ; '
' Mr. Tarte left for London to-night ' ; ' Mr. Tarte has been in London for some days.' And there were significant stories as to the business that took him so frequently to London. Another question-this furniture, which has been charged at $7,641-where is that furniture now ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is there in the office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: What office ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Mr. Fabre's office in Paris.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: This was bought and charged to the Paris exposition, and it remains there now that the Paris exposition is over. Is that furniture needed there-$7,641 worth ? If so, what did Mr. Fabre do before it arrived ? Did he sit up all night in a chair ? Of course, the government did not get those rooms for nothing. What was the rental of them ? I do not see it charged in the account. Was that part of the $109,000 for the particulars of which, the First Minister tells us, we shall have to wait another year ? Is it proposed that the furniture shall remain there, and that this great mansion is to be rented at a high

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: rental, like the old Seybold building here ? The government must give us further particulars. They pretended to make a clean breast of all they knew. They told only what they could not avoid telling. We must have an explanation of this $87,000, less the $10,000, which we have been told has been returned, for that building, which was worth $40,000 or $50,000 according to the Minister of Public Works, but which was not worth more than a quarter of the money according to more competent authority. We want to know what was done with the money of the people of Canada that the Minister of Agriculture, with his usual incapacity, pledged himself two years ago, would be administered economically, which promise he has been utterly powerless to carry out. I would like to ask another question-there are a lot of names here, headed by the Minister of Public Works as chief commissioner, and these other commissioners also spent large amounts of money. I would like to know who was Jas. Jardine, one of the commissioners.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: We produce him-he is here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: What did he do, I would like to know ? When this building was found to be only a worthless barn that did not even keep out the rain from heaven, was there nobody of all these commissioners who could look at it with the eagle eye of the Minister of Public Works and know that the roof would leak, and that it was an improper building to hold the exhibits of Canada ? Now, Mr. Chairman, we shall have to have these two ministers give us a little more information about the way the $315,000 of the people of Canada was squandered.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I always like to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace). He is unique. In my long experience I have never met such a character as he. It takes a man of some ability to make a speech such as the one he has just delivered-ability of a certain order which, perhaps, not many people would like to possess. If the hon. gentleman knew a little more of the world, the world that was in Paris, and is to be found at any exhibition of this kind, he, even he, would not have ventured to say what he has said to-night. Canada is a great country, and her people would not like her to appear in the eyes of the world as a beggarly country. There were many eminent people from all parts of the world in Paris. All the nations represented in Paris had their buildings and offices, ' appartements,' to use the French word, which. I believe, is English also. England had large space in all the buildings, and besides that, in Avenue de la Bourdonais, Col. Jekyll had appartements much larger than the Canadian ones. We took advantage of the Canadian agency in

Paris, which is located at 10 Rue de Rome. It was furnished with decency, as Canada has to be treated everywhere, so that we might be able to receive people who called upon us. I was there most of the time receiving people from all parts of the world, including, of course, the Canadians who visited Paris-1 am glad to say we saw thousands and thousands of them. The Canadians who came to Paris had a right to be received somewhere, had a right to have rooms where they could read or write or transact business. I wish the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) had gone to Paris. He would have seen that all the nations spent vast amounts of money in entertaining. I am sorry that I ever accepted the position of Canadian commissioner in Paris, and I will tell you why. We were invited everywhere, entertained everywhere, but. with the limited amount of money I had at my disposal, we were not able to do honour to this country as we should have been able to do. We can be reproached for nothing except that we did not know what was going to take place in Paris. Instead of spending what we have spent, we should have spent a good deal more. Think of what that exhibition has done to advertise Canada. There are even in this country business firms who spend $500,000 a year in advertising. I know a firm in Canada in which one of our senators is interested, which spent last year $1,000,000 in advertising. The Paris exhibition was a great advertisement for Canada. Was it not reasonable, was it not decent, was it not our duty to have rooms there furnished in a decent manner to receive the visitors who were calling for information ? The furniture that was purchased is the property of this country ; and if the hon. gentleman ever goes to Paris-I wish to God he would go sometimes, because he would learn a little refinement, which he so sorely needs.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: He will take no lessons in that from the Minister of Public Works, nor in integrity either.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I think any lesson I would give him would be altogether lost. I have not the slightest intention to teach him any lesson. But this I must resent-when I hear a man who was nearly becoming a minister speak as he does to-night, I say that the country should not stand it. He has said things which I would characterize, if the word was parliamentary, as being a disgrace to this Canadian parliament. We are not such a small country after all that other nations should look upon us as not understanding our duty. The hon. gentleman has again referred to my London trips. I did go to London on several occasions. If I understood him right he has spoken about 1 ominous stories' as to what led me to London. I do not like to have any misunderstanding, I like plain language. If the hon. gentleman has heard any 'ominous stories' let him tell
those stories in the House. This is the proper place.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I will do it at the proper time, never fear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The proper time is now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am the judge of that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman speak out-speak now. I have nothing to hide either in my public life or in my private life. If the hon. gentleman has anything to say, let him say it now. I know one gentleman who, last year, was villain enough to circulate stories in this parliament. He is no more a member of the House, and he won't come back here for some time. Let us have plain speaking between members of the House. Sir, the hon. gentleman has spoken of my commissioners, he has slighted one of them, Mr. Jardine. Mr. Jardine is not here. He has been a most painstaking commissioner in Paris. There was abundance of work for all of them, and they have performed their work successfully and zealously. I am glad on this occasion to bear testimony to the success and energy with which they performed all their duties.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I feel proud that Canada took so honourable a position at the Paris exhibition, and that even the province of Prince Edward Island made a creditable show of its products. But we are very sorry that such an enterprise as the Paris exhibition should have been prostituted to such political debauchery as the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) has brought to the notice of the House to-night. I think, Mr. Speaker, it would have been a good thing if the roof of that building had fallen in on some of them, rather than that such disclosures should have been made to the people of this country. Now, what are the facts in this connection ? The Minister of Agriculture treated the affair in a light manner. I have before me the declaration of a respectable gentleman, made in regard to this Pineau matter, and I am going to read it to the House, because it is well that the House should have a true understanding of the state of the case :
I, William Callaghan, of Ebbsfleet, Prince county, province of Prince Edward Island, do solemnly declare that on or about February 9 last, Henry J. Pineau, M.L.A., of Ebbsfleet, called on me and said that he wished to speak to me on an important matter, and wanted my advice. He stated to me that he was approached by Dr. Wickham, of Tignish, and was offered, if he would accept, that he- (Mr. Pineau) could get the appointment of commissioner to the Paris exposition with the pay of $5 per day and all expenses. He further stated that Dr. Wickham told him he would have to go to Charlottetown to see Premier Farquharson, who would direct him to the Deputy Minister of Public Works, Ottawa, for further instructions. I told him he was adopting a dangerous course, and better mind what he was about, and go to Tig-

nish and see his friends, which he promised to do. He said it would be a great thing for him to see his own country-Prance. I afterwards saw Mr. Pineau. He told me that he had a letter in his pocket, and his appointment was all right, to date from April 15 to December 1, 1900.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously, believing it to be true, and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act, 1893.
(Sgd.) WILLIAM CALLAGHAN.
Declared before me at Ebbsfleet, Prince county, province of Prince Edward Island, this 28th day of May, A.D. 1900.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.

speechtext:
J.P. for Prince County.
Now, we have also another declaration to the same effect, and then we have the following letter from Mr. Pineau himself :
Ottawa, March 8, 1900.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Shea,
Dear Sir,-I now take the pleasure of writing you a few lines to let you know that I am in Ottawa at present, and I must also tell you that it is a fine place. I have seen a good deal already. I must also tell you that I have been well received by the government here, and I am weighting for orders to go on which I think will be to-morrow or next day I was all over and Seen all the House of Parliament the House of Commons and the Senate Chamber and I must say it is a fine Place to see. it is no wonder that they are so Keen to get here, you keep my C.M.B.A dewes paid up I will send you money in a few days the 10 lb. twine I got from you you can get it Back you can also get your men Boarded at our place if you want and See that they have what they want. You give them what is right for Boarding them I Know you will do that you can tell them at Home if you See them that you got a letter from me I Suppose Some people are very mad at^rne for doing what I have done I Could not Help Myself it is what every man is doing looking out for himself not more at Present I Remain yours truly
I will write you in a few days and will give you more in detail

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.

speechtext: Now, there is a letter of the gentleman himself, and you have the sworn affidavits of two reliable persons. The history of the matter is simply this. The government of Prince Edward Island had lost the confidence of the people, and in consequence a number of by-elections. There was a byelection to be held in the first district of Prince and the life of the Farquharson administration depended upon winning that seat.^ They lost the seat, but the Dominion elections were coming on, and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, 1 presume, was very anxious to keep the local government in power on the island so as to give him a little prestige. So negotiations were entered into, and they sent this Dr. Wickman to this man Pineau, who was financially embarrassed at the time, and the result was that they got him spirited away to Ottawa. Nobody knew that he was coming up, but they got him here. He was in communication with the government, and it does not matter whether or not the hon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Minister of Agriculture or the hon. Minister of Public Works gets up and says : I did not know he was here. I did not see him. That has nothing to do with the case providing he was seen by the Deputy Minister of Public Works or by any member who was authorized to approach him. This shows that the deed was perpetrated and that the government had a hand in that transaction. Will these hon. gentlemen get up and declare before the committee that they knew of no man from Prince Edward Island being up here

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Who was seeking a position of some emolument in order to be paid for some deed he was doing on the island ? I think the matter should not be treated so lightly, and I think the hon. Minister of Agriculture and the hon. Minister of Public Works should get up and tell how much of this money credited to the Paris exhibition was paid for the people of Canada, and how they excuse the expenditure of $312,000 for advertising Canada and doing other things when we know that they were prostituting the money of the people of this country to the uses of political debauchery. I think the expenditure needs more explanation than the hon. Minister of Agriculture has given to the committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, since you have allowed a little extraneous matter to be thrown into the discussion, I would ask for time to throw a little extraneous matter back in reply. The hon. member from the western part of Prince Edward Island (Mr. Haekett) has referred to Mr. Pineau, you may be surprised to know that I also know a little about Mr. Pineau. Perhaps the hon. gentlemen opposite would like to know how we got the information we have. I am sorry I cannot take them into my confidence. However, I am willing to deal with a few occurrences. It is stated that Pineau came to Ottawa. I do not know whether that is so or not. It was actually stated that he came under the malign influence of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), or of his private secretary.' I do not know whether that is so or not, but I am informed on what I consider indisputable evidence that in the interest of hon. gentlemen opposite that hon. gentlemen opposite sent a spy, a detective, after this man Pineau to Boston.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
This I do know that a man went down and met Pineau after rather a difficult hunt, and he said, so I am informed: Pineau, you want money. You have been brought under the influence of the Liberals, but we have as much money as they have, and we can furnish you with what is necessary for you to go back to Prince Edward Island, and put yourself right with your own party. Now, let me say that I know that an
9G1

agent was in direct communication witli a gentleman who is a very prominent factor in the Conservative party, who was so important a man in the Conservative party that he was selected to play a very important part in the late elections.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) knows very little about the matter. Where does he get his information ? Who was the spy he spoke about ? Surely the hon. gentleman was not the spy himself ? Did he go to Boston himself ? He was in the pay of the government, he was supporting them, and while he was working in connection with the bait freezers was he hunting up Pineal! at the same time ? Pineau was paid as my hon. friend says. All I have to say is that we in Prince county, a little over a year ago, elected Pineau to go to the legislature of Prince Edward Island to oppose the Farquliarson government, and, that fresh from the people, he was seduced from his allegiance and taken away and bribed by the present government to support their friends in Prince Edward Island. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) knows very well about the case. He says that Pineau was approached by a Conservative who said that we had as much money as the other side, and that we were going to buy him to support us. Why should we, the people who elected Pineau, be obliged to buy him? He was elected by the free votes of Prince county. This man was debauched. He was brought here by the government, and was held in the shadow of these buildings for a week, and told that he would be sent to Paris. My hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Defurgey) has read to the committee a letter sent to a friend in Prince Edward Island. He has also read a declaration made by a reputable gentleman in West Prince, who swore to the statement made by Pineau that he was to go to Charlottetown to Mr. Farquliarson, and that he would be directed by him to the Deputy Minister of Public Works in Ottawa. That statement has not been refuted by any evidence on the other side. It is a blot upon the fair fame of the country that we should have a government that would buy a man like this. If the government cannot hold power by the intelligent votes of the electors of this country they have no right to hold power at all, and when we find that this government is assisting a local government to maintain power it is a shame and a disgrace that should not be upheld by the people of this country. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) may think that lie is entitled to some consideration in this House. If he has been going around hunting Pineau, if he has been the spy, he should be condemned. The Auditor General's Koport shows that he has received thousands of dollars of the people's money in connection with these bait freezers. Is he the man who, 31
through Dr. Wickham, approached Pineau, and if we believe his statement we must believe that he followed him to Boston with the bait in his pocket, and gave it to him to support the local government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am authorized by the Deputy Minister of Public Works who is now on the floor of parliament to say that he does not know Pineau, and that he has never seen him, and I am adding on my owrn behalf that I would like to know where Pineau is now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I may say in reply to the hon. member from West Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Hackett), that I do not think he is serious when he asks if I was the spy employed by the Conservative party to hunt up Pineau. In the second place, I tell him that the man who was employed in that work undertook to carry a constituency in this country with no other qualification than his bank account, and later, if necessary, we can demonstrate this.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to call your attention, for a moment, to the fact that the last speaker (Mr. Kendall) is scarcely a disinterested witness in this House. The Auditor General's Report contains a record of the hon. gentleman's transactions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Read it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I am going to read it for the benefit of the hon. gentleman, and, perhaps he will not be quite so fresh when I have done.
Mr. DEPUTY Sr-eAKER. I would ask hon. gentlemen to keep as near the discussion of the item under the consideration of the committee as possible. I think we have been wandering away from the point under discussion. I would appeal to hon. gentlemen to keep within a reasonable limit of the question before us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I bow with great pleasure to your ruling, but I would like to know if you have laid down one set of rules for some gentlemen

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Order.
Mr. CLANCY-I am asking a very proper question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I said I bowed to the hon. gentleman's ruling, and then I have a right to ask his reasons for that ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I had no special reference to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) more than to any other member. We have been wandering away from the question before the committee, and I would appeal to members on both sides to keep as near to the discussion as possible. That Is my ruling.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: A reference to Pineau who was engaged to go to Paris, is quite within the question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: He was not engaged.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.

speechtext:
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, that we Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
have heard enough of Mr. Pineau, and I will say nothing further on the subject. There are, however, matters connected with the Paris exposition of which I wish to speak. The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) quoted certain individuals who apparently have been to Paris and have expressed their opinion against the good name of the Canadian exhibit. I was surprised to hear such expression of opinion, because during last summer when I was unfortunately prevented by pressure of other business from going to Paris. I took every possible means of seeking information from Canadians who had been to Paris, and I watched the press carefully to see what opinions were published in regard to the Canadian exhibit. I was extremely gratified to find from private individuals occupying high positions in this country and abroad, from gentlemen intimately connected with the party opposed to us politically, as well as from those who are entirely indifferent to politics ; a universal consensus of opinion that the Canadian exhibit at Paris was a credit to Canada, and that it was a surprise to people from other countries who previously did not understand or appreciate the material and industrial progress of our country during the last few years. I felt that the Canadian exhibit at Paris was costing a considerable amount of money, and that if it did not fulfil its object, this would have been an unjustifiable and extravagant expenditure. I felt myself to a large extent responsible for that expenditure, but from the knowledge that has come to me, I have no hesitation in justifying before the House and before the people, that expenditure, and, Sir, had we spent much more I would have been ready to justify it, because of the vast beneficial results achieved for Canada. I have heard encomiums from Canadians who have gone to Paris, and from foreigners who were sent by their various governments to examine into the economic condition of their rivals in the great commercial markets of the world. I have the testimony here that our Canadian exhibit was one of the most successful in its economic aspects of all the exhibits at the Paris exhibition. In the gathering together of the exhibits, the Canadian commssioners adopted the view that we should not make a flash exhibit of pastimes and side shows to attract the ordinary vulgar crowd for amusement sake, but that we should make an exhibit of the economic products of Canada, so that those who wanted to buy raw material or manufactured products would be lead to make inquiries in Canada for commercial purposes, and to place orders here which would redound to our profit commercially. That was the object with which the exhibits were gathered together, and that object I commended. I took upon myself as Minister

of Agriculture to see that in four great classes the department over which I have the honour to preside, should he worthily represented. We collected an agricultural exhibit, a horticultural exhibit, a mineral exhibit, and an exhibit of forestry, and of fishery and game products, and we put these exhibits collectively before the world, and I am proud to know that as a result every one of these exhibits obtained the grand prix, the highest award possible at the Paris exposition.
In addition to that, we provided the facilities by which the Canadian exhibitors were enabled to go to Paris and exhibit in ordinary competition. We paid the cost of transporting the exhibits to Paris. We paid the expenses of the commissioners, who devoted nearly a year to the preparation of the exhibit, who went through the length and breadth of this country, giving information to the industrial classes, to the agricultural classes, to those engaged in mining, in the fisheries and in forest work ; and by these means we were able to stimulate the people of Canada to make a creditable exhibit. I found, what was a matter of extreme gratification to me, as I am sure it must be to all Canadians, that when our commissioners first went through Canada and asked the people to prepare exhibits for the Paris exhibition, they were told on all sides : We are so busy with the ordinary affairs of commerce, our workshops are so
busy with orders ahead that we can hardly meet these orders, and we cannot afford the time to prepare exhibits for the Paris exhibition. This was a condition of affairs in which we might well rejoice, a condition which had come about within two or three years, but which unfortunately had been unknown in Canada for many years before this government came into power. That was the condition of the industries of the country under this administration in the year 1899-1900 ; but by reason of the value which the Paris exhibition would be to the industries of the country, and by reason of the urgent solicitations of the commissioners, Canada did for the first time in her history make a creditable display of her industrial products and show the world that in many classes of manufacturing she could take a proud position in competition with the other nations of the world. This was a contrast to what she had done a few years before in the Columbian exhibition at Chicago, where every Canadian had to hang his head in shame at the miserably inadequate display which Canadian industries made there. But we were determined to show that Canada could take a position in the industrial world of which she need not be ashamed ; and the result has fully justified our confidence. I have the long list of awards which were given to the Canadian exhibits at Paris, and I will read it to the House :

Although this is an extraordinary showing, I have still to make an explanation to show that it is more important than at first glance it might appear to be. A large number of these Grand Prix and gold medals were given for what are known as collective exhibits. In other countries these collective exhibits were not so largely made use of; but our competitors were individual exhibitors and in that way they got a much larger number of prizes. For instance, our fruits were collective exhibits, made either by provinces or by the Dominion, and these collective exhibits could only obtain one Grand Prix for each exhibit. We could have divided each of these collective exhibits over and over again, and in that way have got a Grand Prix for every portion of that exhibit. And I will venture to say, in connection with the fruit exhibit at Paris, that a totally new conception has come into the minds of the people of the continent of Europe as to Canada; that is, for the first time in many generations, the old story of Canada being a few acres of snow has been absolutely and for ever set at rest, and to-day Canada is known to be a land flowing with milk and honey, and the people of that portion of Europe appreciate this country at its true worth.
I have here another statement which I would like to refer to ; for while this statement of our success is absolute, there is a comparison of which we may well feel proud. I have here a comparative list of the awards granted to the Canadian exhibit and those granted to the mother country. In many of these things we would naturally

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
come to the front; but I would be rather surprised to find Canada coming to the front in competition with the old land in certain products which for centuries she has been working up. Take, for instance, books and binding. Great Britain received ten awards, but Canada received five, almost half as many or more in that highly finished product as the mother country was able to secure.
Take musical instruments, Great Britain received three awards but Canada received six, or this young country had doubled the success of the mother land in this line.
Again, in general machinery, in which the old land has for centuries been the leading country in the world. Great Britain received eleven awards and we received three, and that, I think, is a most creditable showing for Canada in this, to her, comparatively new field. '
In carriages and vehicles, the mother land received five awards and Canada eleven, one of which was a grand prix, and there was no such award given Great Britain.
In agricultural implements, in which the mother land entered into keen competition, Great Britain received twenty four awards and Canada twelve.
In horticulture, with the gardens and the soil of England close at hand, right at the doors of Paris, while our products had to come over 3,000 miles, Great Britain received two awards and we three.
In fruits we received altogether 109 awards, and our fruit had to come over 3,000 miles before they could enter into the competition.
In minerals-and I understood an hon. gentleman opposite to say a little while ago that in that line Canada was not properly represented in mineral display

Canada received forty-two awards and the British Isles only fourteen. In other words, we trebled their success.
In hunting apparatus, we received six awards against Great Britain's eleven, and in the clothing trade we received eleven against her twenty. In the manufacture of paper, we received three against Great Britain's four, and in leather manufacture and skins we had three awards against Great Britain's four.
Altogether Great Britain received 853 awards, and we received 394, or very nearly half as many. I venture to say that this is a showing of which every Canadian should be proud, and of which I certainly, ns the minister responsible for the collection of the exhibits and their display in Paris, am proud and have no hesitation in putting before the country without fear of criticism.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman a list of the prizes taken at the Chicago exhibition. He made some unfavourable comments on our exhibit there, and I presume he will read to the House, to be fair, a list of the prizes taken by us at that exhibition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I have not the list. I was not responsible for that exhibition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman is responsible for the statement he has made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I think I know as much about the Chicago exhibition as the hon. gentleman. In certain lines, Canada made a remarkable success, but in the industrial lines, nobody will dispute the fact that Canada's exhibit at Chicago gave to the world the idea that she had no manufacture worthy of the name. In her natural products, she made a splendid showing. And again dn Paris, she made a very gratifying display, but what I want to emphasize' is the fact that in this Paris exhibition, for the first time in the history of Canadian exhibits at any international or foreign exhibition, Canada came to the front as an industrial and manufacturing country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Thanks to the National Policy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman and his friends know well that in 1896 the people of Canada were tired of their administration of the National Policy and expelled them from the government benches, and the wisdom of the people is shown in the fact that four years later, under the wise policy of a Liberal administration, our industries had advanced iu leaps and bounds and we made an exhibit at Paris which has opened the eyes of the world.
Hon. gentlemen opposite find fault with the way in which the money was spent in the Paris exhibition. But the reason is not far to seek. They remember the good old days when they were able to reward their own friends by their lavish expenditure at the exhibition in Chicago, and cannot conceal their chagrin at the fact that these matters are now in the hands of other men who are able to use them to better advantage to the country.
These hon. gentlemen have read letters criticising Canada's exhibit. Let me read a statement which I am sure these hon. gentlemen must admit comes from an unprejudiced source :
It will be surprising if this show in Paris does not draw world-wide attention to Canada's mining.
I think the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) took some exception to our exhibit in that line.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I made no reference to our mineral exhibit.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Then it must be the hon. gentleman's understudy, the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule). I sometimes mix the one with the other.

And the enormous possibilities in the investment of capital. There is no display of mineral wealth from any country represented in the Paris exhibition except the United States which can for a moment compare with that of Canada, and certainly never before has so large, varied and rich a show of mineral from any single colony been seen in any international exhibit.
The same article goes on to say :
In the little space allowed to Canada, the Commissioners have visibly displayed raw material as most likely to attract attention to the immense forest wealth of Canada ... It would be difficult for England to make a better show of elementary and intermediate education, and in some respects Canada puts the old country to shame.
A little while ago some hon. gentlemen on the other side said our educational exhibit was not worthy of the country, but as a matter of fact, in primary education, Great Britain received only 33 awards and Canada 18, and Canada got high awards for her primary, intermediate and university exhibits. Now here is another extract:
In some departments Britain was foremost, but generally speaking she has allowed it to appear that France, Germany and America are the three great commercial countries and that France is the great colonizer. Canada, however, has put her best foot foremost, and with that loyalty to the empire and the interests of her own people which distinguishes her in these days among the younger nations, she has set up at the Trocadero a show of her industries and boundless resources which will advertise her throughout the world. Her corner of the exhibition is at all times one of the liveliest of the whole show and in proportion to its size perhaps attracts more real business than any other.
That is taken from the Mail and Empire of August 29, sent by its special correspondent at the Paris exhibition. There is another thing I would like to put before the House :
A comparative estimate of the value of Canada's exhibit can only be formed after seeing the products and industries of other countries.
A comparative estimate of the value of Canada's exhibit can be formed only after seeing the products and industries of the other countries. It is gratifying to be able to state that from a commercial point of view, our Dominion leads the whole exposition. This is a testimony of many competent judges, including a number of Frenchmen. We have not the rich and artistic products which dazzle the eyes in the pavilions of the foreign powers, but we have a greater number and variety of useful manufactures than any other country. The number of grand prix which have fallen to our share will be a surprise to many. We have already won the highest awards in forestry, fish and game, agriculture, canoes and minerals, and it is more than likely that the grand prix will also be given to our bicycles and agricultural implements, which are in the annex at Vincennes. That article is from the Montreal Daily Star of July 21, 1900-again a moment of clear vision accorded to the blind. The Montreal Gazette of August 25 says :
Cold storage good

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite sometimes twit me a little with the failure of cold storage, but the Montreal Gazette says my exhibit in Paris was an excellent one.
A large stand, showing Canadian apples, &e., gathered last fall and preserved in the cold storage, attracted great attention. Cold storage is not familiar yet to the crowds, who would * hardly credit that the fine specimens of apples were not wax imitations. Had the French commissioners granted sufficient room, it was the intention of the Canadian commissioners to make cold storage a very prominent exhibit. As it is, all that is to be seen of this marvellous invention is in a little out of the way cellar, where the Linde British Refrigeration Co., of London and Montreal have their system in operation.
And then he goes on to describe the exhibit we have there. Now, let us take extracts from other papers. I have here a statement from the Manitoba Free Press, with the testimony of a prominent citizen of Winnipeg, Dr. McArthur. I do not know the gentleman, but he says :
Canada had the finest display of natural products. Canada had the only cold storage exhibit on the grounds and it excited a great deal of interest.
Here is a statement from a French newspaper, which, to save the nerves of hon. gentlemen opposite, I will not read. But here are one or two statements which I will take almost at haphazard from a large number. I find, from gentlemen who have had experience in exhibition work, and who have no connection with Canada or the Canadian commission in any shape or way. For instance, Mr. B. I. Bose, commissioner for British India, our rivals in the exhibition, occupying the adjoining building to us, and naturally desirous to putting forward their claims, says :-
With over twenty-live years' experience of international exhibitions, I can without hesitation testify that Canada's representation at Paris this year is the best and most perfect that the Dominion has ever made and I believe will result in a great increase of her trade. The elaborate statistical and other works (printed, in both French and English) dealing with the products and resources of the country compare most favourably with those of all other countries and reflect the greatest credit on the government of the Dominion.
(Signed) B. I. ROSE, Commissioner for British India. Here is a gentleman who is engaged in trade in England, and whose business is especially interesting to us, because he is interested in the produce trade-Mr. Walter Stark :
I have been exceedingly pleased in looking over Canada's exhibits, and must say it does both the producers, and those who have been responsible for display, very much credit. Such a splendid display of Canada's products must be an eye opener to Europe and should be of great service to the Dominion.
Here is a French gentleman of special qualifications as a representative of the Chambre

de Commerce de Lyons, and I am afraid, even though it grates on the feelings of hon. gentlemen opposite, I shall have to read it :
Paris, October, 1900.
Having been intrusted by the Chamber of Commerce, of Lyons, to gather the elements of a collection of samples, in connection with the industrial and agricultural production of Canada,
I have received from Mr. Auguste Dupuis, the secretary of the Canadian section at the Paris Exposition, all desirable data and information. The Chamber of Commerce, of Lyons, would receive with acknowledgments any collection it would please the Dominion government to send them.
(Signed) F. VERTAN.
So, here we have an anticipation on the part of a French gentleman, representing the Chambre de Commerce de Lyons, of a large augmentation of the trade between Canada and France in consequence of the exhibition. Here is another gentleman from France, who was particularly authorized to study the products of foreign countries, and especially of colonies, for the purpose of helping the French government in the development of their colony in Algiers :
Mr. Amedee Rebattu, lumber merchant, from Bone (Algeria), a member of the statistical committee of the ' Algerian Statistical Union ' and a member of the jury (class 90) at the exhibition of 1900, asks for information concerning the use and manufacture of cold storage appliances for the preservation of fruit.
He came to us for information and specimens in regard to cold storage. Here is another gentleman, the assistant commissioner general of Great Britain :
Paris, Nov. 29, 1900.
X am delighted to be afforded this opportunity of placing upon record my admiration for the successful manner in which the work of the Canadian section of the Paris exhibition has been carried out.
The installation of the exhibits, combined the most remarkable illustrations of the industrial wealth and progress of the Dominion with general artistic effect which it would be difficult to surpass, whilst the courtesy and experience of the organizers naturally contributed in the highest degree to the success of the'section.
(Signed) EDMUND R. SPEARMAN
Assistant commissioner general of Great Britain.

I have much pleasure in bearing witness to the admirable display made by Canada at the exhibition. In the magnificent show of Canada's industries and products at the Trocadero, I was enabled to see a striking corroboration of what I had previously read in magazines and other publications. I am delighted to have this opportunity of testifying to the same.

15 rue des Augustins, Bruxelles.
In charge of the information service for the export of agricultural products from Belgium.

My friends and I are greatly pleased with the Canadian exhibit and I, who with dear love remember my old home, rejoice to realize my country's improvement, development and increasing prosperity.
(Signed)

The thoroughly practical character of the exhibit combined with effective and tasteful arrangement (which is in itself a work of business capacity) cannot fail to strike the observer with highly favourable impressions.
In my own case these impressions are of course made peculiarly agreeable, because of the many pleasant associations awakened by renewed acquaintance with typical products of the country which must hold a firm place in the regard of those who have partaken of the hospitality of * Our Lady of the Sunshine.' [DOT]
(Signed) ABERDEEN.

I am delighted to be afforded this opportunity of congratulating our brethren of Canada upon their magnificent and most interesting industrial and agricultural exhibit.

The fruit exhibit is admirable and defies description. I shall be delighted to know the names and addresses of the various fruit producers and to represent some of them in Paris. Being an agent for food products, I could easily place those products on the market, and especially canned fruit in the natural state, such as peaches, plums, raspberries and apricots.
(Signed) E. CERF, Agent for food products.

I have visited most parts of the world, and I believe the Canadian display of fruit at Paris exhibition is the finest I have seen.
(Signed)
CHEVALIER KENN DE HOVGERWOERD, Consul General in Turkey, Persia, Arabia,
Siam, etc., Les Sources, Champagne, Seine-et-Oise, France.

Being a manufacturer of preserves, am highly pleased with Canadian show of fruit. Shall at any time be pleased to receive lists, &c.

Birmingham, England.

I am surprised at the great variety of fruits and qualities. No one certainly who had not visited Canada would dream of the variety and beauty.

Absolutely the best show of fruit in the exhibition, which is a great and pleasant surprise to find.

speechtext:
That alcohol was bought for the purpose of preserving fruit. And here I would like to mention, since the hon. gentleman has brought the subject forward, that one of the most effective and remarkable exhibits in the Paris exhibition was the fruit exhibit. We were able, by reason of the excellent management of Prof. Saunders, of the Experimental Farm, who had charge of that particular exhibit, to collect in the autumn of 1899, fruit from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia. The fruit was carefully collected by chosen agents throughout the orchards of Canada, and sent into cold storage in the city of Montreal in the autumn of 1899. It was kept in Montreal until the spring of 1900, it was then picked over again, packed and sent over in our cold storage departments on the steamers to Liverpool. It was sent by express from Liverpool to Paris, and put into our cold storage chambers in the Paris exhibition. That fruit was able to go out, after a passage from British Columbia, of over G.000 miles, to Paris, in our cold storage arrangements, to come into competition with the fresh fruits of Europe, to beat them and to obtain the highest awards which were granted to any fruit on exhibition at Paris. During the summer of 1900 we again collected fresh fruit in Canada and again sent specimens of the large fruit of all the provinces in the Dominion. Again we were able to come into competition with the fresh fruits of Prance, Germany, England, Belgium and all the European countries,

sent straight from their own orchards by express only a few days' journey to Paris, and again Canada succeeded in beating the world and getting a larger number of awards than was given to any other country for fresh fruits. This is remarkable testimony not only to the quality of the fruit production of Canada, but to the perfection of the cold storage transportation facilities which were provided by the government for the benefit of the producers in Canada in puting their wares on the foreign markets. I do not know if there is any particular necessity for my saying anything more on these matters. If particular information is desired, I shall be glad to give all I have at my disposal. I will say this, however, that in connection with this exhibition, in connection with all the expenditure in regard to it, with every item and every detail, I am perfectly willing that the truth should be known that hon. gentlemen opposite should sift it to the bottom. I am satisfied, and know that in the hands of the commissioners who had it in charge, appointed by this government, the expenditure has been absolutely and entirely proper, correct, pure and free from any scandal whatever, and I will challenge an inquiry on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, by themselves, or in any way they can conduct it, to find out if there is anything different from what I say.

Miss Barry was one of several of the staff who were asked by me to contribute to Canadian papers, articles 5" connection with what was going on at Paris in connection with the Pains exhibition. I cannot tell what their private arrangements may have been, but their instructions were that they should not do so. Miss Barry was appointed as an assistant to Madame Danduraud, the lady commissioner to represent Canada at these gatherings of the women of the world which took place in Paris. I may say that several organizations of the ladies of this country requested that at Paris the women of Canada should be recognized and represented. I believe it was in the interest of Canada that this should be done, and therefore I took upon myself to recommend the appointment of the honorary lady commissioner Madame Danduraud, who is

well known in literary circles in Canada for her writings on many subjects, was chosen, and she represented Canada most worthily. She is a lady of not only high social position in Canada, but of literary accomplishments as well, and possessed of what the French call esprit, which we can hardly translate, and which I would not like to translate in connection with a lady.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to interrupt Mm a moment. Miss Barry has been allowed living allowance, and that is now a system which is carried on all through the service. It is a system which has created a breach between the Auditor General and the government of the day. I do not believe that those in the service of the government should in any sense receive mean or beggarly treatment in relation to their expenses, and I can quite understand that in certain cases it might not be wise that the accounts of persons occupying certain positions should be published to the world. I wish to point out this case, because it is becoming the habit of this government to allow living expenses which are equivalent to part of a salary. I see that Miss Barry is allowed the maximum of $6 a day. While she no doubt occupied an important position, I do not understand that she occupied a position justifying that allowance. Under the former government all accounts were rendered, and hon. gentlemen opposite were manly and courageous enough to criticise them, even to the pay of bootblacks and other incidental expenses which are no doubt included in these living allowances, and they were spread all over ail the backwoods of Canada in order to discredit the government. Whether these expenses were excessive or not may be open to debate; but the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite have covered them up in living allowances is something that cannot be condoned. I think this committee should lay down a rule by which every person in the service not occupying a responsible position should render an account, so that this House might see it. The hon. gentleman is in error. The $8 covered both salary and living expenses. It was allowed to all below the rank of commissioner, except the labourers, who were employed there and paid by the day. A large number of employees were paid at the uniform rate of $6 a day, which covered all they received during the time they were in Paris. Besides that, their actual transportation charges from here to Paris and back were paid. The commissioners went into this matter very thoroughly before fixing the remuneration. In most cases the employees protested against it; but it was felt that it would be a fair return for their labour in a foreign country, where, of
course, they would be under unusual expenses. Everybody knows that on the occasion of a great exhibition like that, the cost of living is greatly increased, and we could not expect them to live in Paris as economically as in Ottawa or elsewhere in Canada. In a rough awy, I may say, this $6 a day was thought to be about equally divided between living allowance and salary. The ordinary living allowance made by the government to people of that class while travelling abroad is, I understand, $5 a day. That was before the present arrangement was made with the Auditor General by which actual disbursements were charged. But in this case the Auditor General has gone over all these accounts, and has accepted this arrangement as being a satisfactory one.

Dawson, whose death the other day is such a great loss to this whole Dominion, aud especially to the department of which he was the brilliant head, and in which he has given so much excellent and invaluable work to the Dominion of Canada. Speaking as one who has come largely into contact with his work in connection with this Paris exhibtion, I may say that if Canada made the splendid record she did with her mineral exhibit, it was largely due to the experience and wide knowledge exercised by Dr. Dawson in the preparation and management of that exhibit.
