speechtext:
I think it would be unfair to attack a man who is not in this House to defend himself. But it is quite as unseemly to import here a man whose name appears in the public accounts in order that he may protect and coach the minister. No more unseemly thing has ever happened in this House. I do not kuow anything about Mr. Jardine, but it is reported that he has taken very active part in the elections.
Man after man in Canada, good officials, have been dismissed, their moneys that were paid into the public treasury taken from them, faith not kept with them-and for what V Because it has been charged, but never proved in a single instance, that they had taken part in elections. Yet, a gentleman is on the floor of this House this evening, prompting the minister, who has earned his position by political activity -as has been stated uublushingly by the Minister of Agriculture that that was his special qualification to be appointed to this office. If we hope to get these estimates through, and I do for one, we must not have the unseemly conduct of the Minister of Agriculture. We have a good deal too much of this by-play. The hon. gentleman has done a good deal of acting, a good deal too much, for it was bad acting. His deportment has not contributed very much, I will not say to increase his reputation, but to maintain the traditions of the high place he occupies. The hon. gentleman challenges any on this side to bring forward a single administrative act that was not clean or that will not bear the search-light of inquiry. And yet he declares, backed up by the Minister of Public Works, that there was an open swindle upon the people of Canada, and that nobody is responsible for it. No hon. minister can shelter himself behind the High Commissioner. If the hon. minister is in a position in .which he has no redress, it must be because he failed to take the necessary precautions that should
le taken by one acting for the country in a case of that kind. But the hon. gentleman came here with a statement that he has been told by the High Commissioner to pay the bill, and say nothing about it. Why ? Is it because there is a reflection upon the High Commissioner as a member of the Imperial commission ? I will not reflect upon Lord Strathcona, but, as the hon. leader of the opposition says, this is a matter of business concerning which the people's representatives should know the facts. If there are reasons why we should pay the bill and ask no questions, the hon. minister should be able to give those reasons.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. gentlemen opposite have asked with regard to a number of others than those I have already mentioned

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Before the hon. minister proceeds, I will ask him to explain why it was that no action was taken beyond the writing of the letter of Lord Strathcona, of which he speaks, to inquire into that swindle and to get the reparation to which Canada is entitled.
I he MINISTER OF AGRlOLx,.. RE. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) was probably absent from the Chamber when I answered that question, when asked by the leader of the opposition. I explained that the control of the building was in the hands of the Imperial commission, on which Lord Strathcona was our representative. They felt that we ought to pay, and insisted on our paying. We could look to them, but we have no recourse elsewhere. We had undertaken to make an exhibit at Paris under the condition, which was stated in the first place, that we should deal through the Imperial authorities. When my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Public Works went to France, he succeeded in obtaining for us a superior position to that which had been accorded before, and this fact, I have uo doubt contributed largely to the success of our exhibit. I would have been glad could that have been the case from the commencement; but it was not. The building referred to was not a Canadian, but a Colonial building, in which we had only part of the space; and we and the other colonies entrusted the management of the building entirely to the Imperial commission, through whom we did all our work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I was in when the hon. minister (Mr. Fisher) made his previous statement, and he has told me nothing new. But when this swindle was discovered- and that is a mild term to apply to it-was there any correspondence to show that the High Commissioner, who was one of the Imperial commissioners, protested or made this a subject of inquiry into the fraud perpetrated upon Canada ? If there is any

point of that kind on which the hon. gentleman has correspondence or is prepared to make an authoritative statement, we would like to hear from him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has already been informed that the hon. Minister of Public Works, when he went to Paris, protested

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Permit me-I am asking if the High Commissioner representing Canada protested against Canada being compelled to pay an undue sum for services she did not receive, and If the High Commissioner, both as High Commissioner for Canada and as a member of the Imperial commission, endeavoured to make this a subject of inquiry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Perhaps I can give a word of explanation. As my hon. friend and colleague said, I protested as soon as I found that the specifications had not been followed. The architect admitted that they had not been followed. With that admission I immediately wrote to Lord Stratlicona, and after negotiating, Sir Montague Ommany, Under Secretary of State for the Colonies, came to Paris. We discussed the question. I represented that the building was not worth what was contracted for. After giving all the attention we could to the question, Sir Montague Ommany, who is a lawyer and a man of long experience, said that we were altogether without any recourse because the architect had given certificates to Messrs. Humphreys & Co., the builders. We withheld for some time a larger amount of money than was agreed for, so as to oblige the builders to make repairs if any accident happened.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I understand it was the High Commissioner's special business as representing Canada, and one in a position to examine, to know whether the architect was justified in giving the contractor a certificate. Again, I ask the question if the hon. gentleman is aware that the High Commissioner made any attempt to make this a subject of inquiry ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am sure that the High Commissioner used his best endeavours to settle that difllculty. But it was found that the architect had given certificates against which we could not rebel. My colleague had nothing to do but to pay it. The bottom of the whole difficulty lay in the fact that we were not masters of the situation, the Royal Commission were the masters of the situation. Mr. Clewes, the architect, was recommended to Lord Strathcona as a reliable man, and he was very much surprised, and the Royal Commission were very much surprised, when they found that the building was not what it should have been.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman aware by personal knowledge that the High Commissioner, at any stage, protested or made this a subject of inquiry ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes, he did.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: By correspondence ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes, I know he has communicated with my colleague, and I will produce the correspondence in a day or two, all that is in my hands.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: And the correspondence, as I understand, will show that the High Commissioner not only entered his protest but also made it a subject of inquiry ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes, so much so that Sir Montague Om-maney came to Paris on purpose to investigate the difficulty.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman a report of the investigation ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No. Sir Montague Ommaney did not make a written report, as he was not bound to do so. The Royal Commission were the masters of the situation, we complained, but more than that we could not do. The building was nearly completed when I reached Paris, and I was astonished at the character of the building. I called the attention of Mr. Clewes and of the contractors to the state of the building, and I forced from Mr. Clewes the admission that the specification had not been followed. He said that he vainly endeavoured to oblige Humphries & Co. to carry out their work in the way it should be done. Then I asked him if he had notified the Royal Commission, and he said that he had not. Then I told him that he had not done his duty, and I wrote to Lord Strathcona and to the Royal Commission stating all these facts. My letters will be found in the correspondence that will be brought down. Lord Strathcona then interfered and Sir Montague Ommaney came to Paris.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: At whose instance ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: He was sent by the Royal Commission. I made a mistake when I said that he was a lawyer, he is an engineer, as he told me himself. Sir .Montague told me that from a legal standpoint our hands were tied, that we could not do anything, that the architect had got several letters that were binding. The architect was responsible to the Royal Commission, he was not appointed by us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman found the building unsatisfactory and not what was required, why did he pay the money ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I did not pay the money. The Imperial government had exacted from this government that we should take part in the exhibition in a certain way. In pursuance of the agreement that was made between the Imperial government and ourselves, the building in Paris was erected without our having any control over it. Indeed, incredible as it may appear, the contractors were left In possession of the building during the whole time of the exhibition, we could not even get possession of the building. I had never before read of specifications or a contract like that, but we could do nothing, we could not close the doors, and we had to go on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Does it not show all through a want of business intelligence and attention? We have already voted $315,000 for the Paris exhibition, and it will probably reach a good deal higher sum. Now, the country expects the ministers in charge to look after these things, to look after the expenditure of that money and to get full value for it. Yet they are obliged to come here and, in a humiliating way, admit that we did not get value for the money, that we in fact had been swindled, and they say nobody is to blame.
The	MINISTER	OF	PUBLIC	WORKS.
I did not say that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Whom should we hold responsible for it ?
The	MINISTER	OF	PUBLIC	WORKS.
The Royal Commission is responsible for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Do we not hold responsible the ministers of the Crown under whose charge the money is spent ?
The	MINISTER	OF	PUBLIC	WORKS.The Imperial government insisted on my hon. friend giving to them the control of the erection of the building. Was it possible for the Minister of Agriculture to foresee that the Royal Commission would commit a blunder like this ? I could not believe my eyes when I saw the building, I could not believe that such a contract could have been given. The Royal Commission trusted their	architect, he	was the
architect not only for our building but for all the Imperial and colonial buildings. I do not want to make any accusation against him, but it seems to me clear that as soon as he found out that he could not bring Messrs. Humphrey & Co. to alter the contract, he should have notified the Royal Commission in London, which he did not do. He admitted to me that he did not do anything of the kind. He was wrong there, but it is for the Royal Commission to deal with him, we are helpless.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: But will not the country hold responsible for it the minister of the [DOT]Crown under whom the money was paid ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The country will hold us responsible to this extent, that we should not have given over the entire control to the Imperial authorities. We are a self-governing country, and we should have gone there and conducted our own business in our own way. We have given up the control of our own building, and to that extent we are guilty. I think it is a fault that we should not be accused of after all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Did the architect ever give an explanation why he passed that building ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I may say that I could not get any satisfactory explanation from him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It seems almost incredible that he should have done that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is just as well that this parliament should know all about it. There is nothing to hide.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am not suggesting-

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am just stating the facts as I know them. The building is not what it should have been, and there has been a miscarriage of justice somewhere. More than that I do not know.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is quite clear that the Imperial Commission trusted the architect, that the architect did not do his duty, that we trusted the Imperial Commission, and that we paid our money and got no return for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Do not say that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: How does that correspond with the statement of the hon. Minister of Agriculture a few minutes ago, that the most conclusive inquiry could be made and that nothing would be found wrong ? And now, we are told that the correspondence, which has not been placed on the Table of the House although it ought to be in the possession of the committee, to enable it to go into this inquiry, has been carried on between the hon. Minister of Agriculture and the High Commissioner, and between the hon. minister and some one else. All this is withheld from the House, although the papers should have been put upon the Table of the House before this inquiry commenced. Certainly the House is entitled to these papers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I think the motion for the papers was only passed the day before yesterday.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
But the hon. minister knew that this estimate was coming up today. and how is the committee intelligently to deal with it in the absence of this cor-

respondeuce ? It could not be expected to do it. The lion. Minister of Agriculture has been justifying himself in regard to everything that has been done, and the whole tenor of his remarks seems to be very much as if he said : Thank God, I am not like other men. The hon. Minister of Agriculture did everything right. He read us certificates of character, and when we asked him whom these statements were from, we found that they were from his own guests, who were invited to write their autographs in his album, with a little puff, after they had probably been wined and entertained. They were written at his request, and in addition, the puffery bureau, like that which has been established in Ottawa, supplied complimentary allusions to himself, and these puffs were sent all over the counry. He says that Miss Barry was one of those so employed. He says: We allowed her to write certain papers, she was under our care, receiving our money. As a consequence she would not be likely to write in a critical strain. In my judgment, we could not expect anything from these persons which would enable us to arrive at a proper conclusion as to whether matters were well conducted or otherwise. The hon. Minister of Agriculture referred to a letter which I read from a gentleman who was in Paris, and he said that it was not in accordance practically with the truth. Well, at least, it was from an independent source, it was from a party who had no interest in either belittling the Canadian exhibit on the one side or of eulogizing it on the other. It is evidence from an independent source, and I need only mention the fact that where there was a creditable exhibit lie said so and made full acknowledgment of the merits of those features of the exhibit which were deserving. I instanced the mineral display, and the hon. Minister of Agriculture told us how many diplomas and awards had been obtained in that line. The gentleman whom I quoted did not complain in regard to that. He said that there was a fairly good display of minerals, but there was no person in connection with it to give that information which should have been available so as to induce capitalists to come to Canada and invest their money in mines. We have no evidence that any such information was given, but the minister says : See the magnificent' results we have achieved ! What results did he give us ? Did he tell us how many orders had been given to Canada for goods as the result of the exhibits, or how much had been sold on account of the display we made ? Not at all ; he did not say a word about that, but he went on to read the certificates of character which had come from this questionable source. If the hon. gentleman had told us that a great many orders had been given for the manufactured articles or the raw products of Canada, I would have said that the information was much more valu-
.Mr. SPROULE.
able than that which he gave us. These complimentary puffs are all right, but they have been well paid for, and the people of the country will know how to appreciate the importance of them. But, there is the undeniable fact that Canada's money has been squandered without any adequate return, and that the ministers admit. They found a building unsuitable for the requirements, but the money had to be paid for it. That is the sum and substance of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I do not propose to detain the committee further than to make a remark in regard to the responsibility of ministers, and of the government, in regard to this transaction. Surely, neither the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte), nor the government of which he is such a distinguished member, can hope to escape that proper ministerial responsibility that attaches to every act and transaction, no matter how remotely they should be connected with it. In the first place the hon. gentleman gives as an excuse and as a reason that it was a mistake to surrender entirely this whole matter into the hands of the Imperial Commission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Why did he do it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That is a matter that involves responsibility, but 1 am not going to discuss that phase of it. The point I desire to make is, that when they surrendered this matter entirely into the hands of the Imperial commissioners, they did it knowing perfectly well that Canada had a representative who was also a member of the Imperial Commission. Now, the government of the day is responsible for every act that the representative of Canada does, either as a member of the Imperial Commission, or as High Commissioner, and the hon. gentleman has as much responsibility as if he did it himself, if it were done through the High Commissioner of Canada, especially as High Commissioner, or as a member of the Imperial Commission. But the hon. gentleman says that there was an inquiry that a Mr. So-and-so came to Paris after this matter had been stirred up, and that the Imperial commissioners, including the representative of Canada, all agreed that nothing could be done. It was the business of the government of Canada, through the Imperial Commission and the High Commissioner, to have made an inquiry and to have punished the offenders. There is absolutely no escape from the ministerial responsibility that attaches to the hon. gentleman and the government of which he is a member. It is perfectly idle for the minister to say it was a mistake to place the authority there. The hon. gentleman knew that he must have trusted some person, and he is responsible for having misplaced his trust.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
The country will not be surprised at this vast unpardonable expenditure, because it was expected that the Paris exposition would be a grand carnival for a number of the Liberals and their

friends. I think the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) was too generous in excusing his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, nor does the fault lie altogether on the shoulders of the Minister of Agriculture, but must be shared in by the Postmaster General, who forced him to appoint this Mr. Jardine, who is utterly unfit for the position of commissioner. I think it is time now for the Minister of Agriculture, in view of my denial, should retract his statement as to the castigation this Mr. Jardine gave me on the public platform, because if that statement does not emanate from his own fertile brain-and that is quite a strain on his brain power-it must be traced to this Mr. Jardine. Who is this Mr. Jardine anyway ? Neither the Minister of Agriculture nor the Minister of Public Works knew anything about his fitness for the job, because he was forced on them by the Postmaster General. The minister told us that Mr. Jardine was selected for his knowledge of trade and commerce. Well, I have the public accounts of the province of Ontario before me, and year after year this gentleman who is so well versed in trade and commerce, occupied the position of what is called a sessional clerk in Toronto, which up there is a happy medium between a page boy and something else. It is a notorious fact that this gentleman for years has been figuring in the Ontario public accounts as a second edition of W. T. R. Preston, the local government hack, and on page after page of the public accounts appears the name of ' Jardine,'
' Jardine,' ' Jardine,' the very same gentleman who figured as a commissioner at Paris.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Sardine.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: An hon. gentleman suggests ' sardine,' and he may have been that too, because I have known him to be in a pretty close box several times. I do not know who authorized this vast expenditure for furniture in Paris, but I am bound to say it was not the Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I had nothing to do with that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I now ask the Minister of Agriculture if it was he who authorized this huge expenditure for furniture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: When I was in Paris the Canadian commissioner, Mr. Pabre, showed me his office, and I found it to be utterly inadequate for what I was sure would be the demands upon it for the exhibition. I authorized Mr. Pabre to secure another office and to furnish it, and he did so. He sent in the accounts and I was told by the commissioners that these accounts were correct, and that the goods were delivered in the manner in which the accounts showed they were.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
If the purchases were made upon the recommendation of Mr. Fabre, then Mr. Fabre got too large a limit altogether. To pay $80 each for sofas and $27 each for chairs is an indecent expenditure of the public money. We have the startling admission made to-night that	the government spent $315,000
upon the exhibition, with the result that from the very day of the opening Canada was black-eyed as to the exhibit she made, and to-night both of the ministers who went to Paris at the expense of the country, are forced to admit that thousands of dollars of this expenditure were entirely uncalled for. Let this be a warning. The Buffalo exhibition is coming on next year, and it is to be hoped that Canada will have a 'proper exhibition there, and that due economy will be practised. If not, the blame will be upon the head of the Minister of Agriculture much more than in the present case. Once again I repeat that the minister made a great mistake when he appointed this Mr. Jardine, who was utterly unfitted for the position he occupied. Just as Mr. Preston of Ontario was dumped on the Minister of the Interior, so Mr. Jardine was dumped on the Minister of Agriculture, and both ministers are entitled to sympathy. I suppose that after all that has been said this item might as well pass.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Does Mr. Pabre occupy these six rooms at the present time ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Mr. Fabre is occupying the same rooms that he and I occupied during the Paris exhibition. They are just comfortable rooms and no more. I know that the expenditure on the furniture may look a little high, but during the exhibition we had to put on airs a little.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Is it necessary to keep up all that style now when the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is not there to represent Canada ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: When one has fallen into decent habits it is difficult to get out of them. The rooms are still there and the furniture is there. The price was a little high, I grant, but at the same time we received thousands and thousands of callers in these rooms, and two or three thousand dollars more or less in a great advertisement of this kind does not amount to much after all. My persanal opinion, apart from all party feeling, is, that the rooms were furnished in a proper way and only in a proper way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Was that furniture made in Canada.?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Surely not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Why not ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It was made in ' gay Paree.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Yes. Speaking of furniture, I think we ought to be able to establish a large market for our furniture in France. I know that orders have already been placed as a result of the exhibition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: If we had sent *our own furniture there, would it not have been an excellent advertisement ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I wish we had done so. I wish we had done what Australia did. They found their building in the same inferior condition as ours, and they imported wood from Western Australia, and rebuilt the entire inside of the building. We talk about spending money for Canada, but the small colony of 'Western Australia with a population of 150,000 people spent a vast sum of money in rebuilding their building. They imported their own architect, their lumber and their furniture, and if I had been there two months before, I think I would have asked my colleague to do the same thing. But it was too late when I arrived there, and we did the best we could. In my opinion we should give more attention to that Paris agency. I believe we could establish a large trade with France and Belgium in fruit, timber, furniture, pulp, paper and other articles. So far we have not perhaps given the Paris agency all the attention we should give it. This exhibition has been a great advertisement for Canada. The Massey-Harris Company will tell you that they are to-day selling agricultural implements in France to the value of millions of francs. I say again, if we only follow up that Paris exhibition, there is a great opening for us. It seems to me lion, gentlemen are going a little too far in criticising my hon. colleague the Minister of Agriculture for things for which after all he is not responsible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Interior if he intends to keep up the magnificent apartments in the city of Paris for the immigration agent there. It seems to me that for all the people we are getting from France, it is hardly worth while to maintain that agency; the money could be better spent in other places. It is certainly not necessary to keep up those extravagant apartments simply for an immigration agent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: So far this House has voted only $2,500 a year for the Paris agency. It is not enough. My hon. friend is altogether mistaken in his views. There is no use of being so much afraid of France ; it is not a bad country.	[DOT]

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am not afraid of France, but how many immigrants a year are we getting from there ? This gentleman has been there for many years at a very large outlay, and what has lie done for his money?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: If you are going to establish an agency there for trade and commerce, that is another tiling^ but if you are simply going to have him as an immigrant agent, it is not necessary to give him such extravagant quarters.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Agriculture did not answer the question of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) as to what Mr. H. O. ICnowiton had done for the $1,115.45 which was paid to him; also what his occupation was, and where he lived.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I was answering all these question when I was interrupted. Mr. ICnowiton lives in my own county. He is a fruit-grower, a business man and a farmer. I appointed him on the Paris staff in consequence of the excellent work which I found he had done at the Omaha exhibition the year before.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: You sent him to Omaha the year before ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I did. I appointed one man from my county on the whole staff in connection with the Paris exhibition.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Then I see on page D- 13, of the Auditor General's Report that $3,000 was paid to J. I. Tarte on account of travelling expenses. I would like to know what trips he made for the $3,000, and what he was paid besides for living expenses ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works was paid altogether $0,000 for his trip and expenses in connection with the Paris exhibition. The $3,000 which is put down for travelling expenses ought to be for general expenses, as should the other amount which is given for living expenses. There was no requirement that part should be paid for travelling and part for living.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: My hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) asked the Minister of Public Works if it was the intention of the government that Mr. Fabre should retain the large office which was obtained for the Paris exhibition, which was probably quite a proper thing to do. His duties in connection with the exhibition have now entirely ceased, and my hon. friend asked if it was the intention that he should still retain those offices, seeing that his duties will be now entirely different from those for which the offices were obtained. I have some hesitation in asking this question, because the hon. Minister of Public Works intimated that if a gentleman from this side of the House asked a question of that kind, he was striking at France. The sooner the hon. gentleman drops that kind of language the better for the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I was joking, as my kon. friend knows.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. gentleman's remarks do not go to the country as a joke; but even as a joke, they are not very happy, in view of a good many things which I do not care to resuscitate or discuss to-night. I ask the hon. gentleman to answer that question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Mr. Fabre is in the same rooms which he occupied during the exhibition. These rooms are one story higher than those he occupied under the late administration for years. There are only two rooms additional. It was found necessary for the exhibition to have the higher flat because there were two rooms additional.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The rent and taxes are over $1,300 a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: But the apartments are in a fine location.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: It is money spent for nothing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should weigh a little more carefully his words. The thousands of English and French Canadians who visit Paris every year will tell him that that agency has been most useful. I admit that we have not received from France as many immigrants as we should like, but we have spent very little money there. This House has voted every year only $2,000, and the vote was originated by the hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Is it the intention to keep on these apartments ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That I do not know. This question will have to be decided later.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman should know, because he is the one who suggested the leasing of them.
The minister of public works.
No, I am not. When I reached Paris I found the rooms occupied and furnished. I simply took possession of one of them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The Minister of the Interior brought down a return showing that from France and Belgium we only got 483 immigrants, and it does not show how many stayed here. In view of that fact, these seem very extravagant offices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I had with me two days ago the representative of a large French syndicate, who have settled in the Yukon, and are conducting large operations there. How have we attracted these men to this country ? By advertising this country and by having an agency in Paris. There is a large amount of French and Belgium capital that could 324
be brought here, and French, English, Belgium and German money is good money.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Were the travelling expenses of the Hon. S. A. Fisher, $526 on page D-5, in conection with the Paris exhibition ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No, they are not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Is Mrs. Turcotte, who had $276 for living allowance, employed in any other capacity ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: She was employed two or three years in the Railway Department and came to my department in 1899 as a typewriter and to prepare the index of my private correspondence. I took her to Paris with my private secretary, Mr. Haines, in the same capacity as that in which she was working with me in Ottawa, namely, as a typewriter and stenographer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Was she a permanent employee ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No, she was not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman got through the explanation of the duties of the different persons which I asked him to give.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I think I got down as far as Col. Gour-deau when I was interrupted. Miss LeBou-thillier was one of the ladies with Miss Galbraith, sent out in charge of the ladies' room and as typewriters to the commissioners. Mr. A. P. Lowe is one of the officers of the Geological Survey. He was on leave of absence in Europe and went to Paris in the place of Mr. Fallardeau, who was returning here. Mr. Macoun is an officer of the Geological Survey and well known for his scientific attainments, and especially his knowledge in connection with forestry. He took charge of the forestry exhibit in Paris. Mr. McKenna was employed under Prof. Robertson to take charge of the food products exhibit in connection with the cold storage. Mr. Perrault is the commissioner appointed from the province of Quebec. He was the first to go over to Paris to receive the goods sent from here. Mr. Scott, another commissioner, was a resident of Winnipeg and represented specially the west. He had been for a number of years representative of Manitoba in Toronto, specially engaged in showing the products and exhibits of Manitoba in the Ontario local exhibitions. I found him a most efficient business-like commissioner, and have appointed him in charge of the Glasgow exhibition. Mr. J. Otis Turcotte is a gentleman from Quebec recommended by Mr. Parent, at the request of Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier, to be the chief of the caretakers and the employees there, to keep their time and

see that they kept the building and exhibits in proper order. Mr. Perrault is a well-known fruit-grower from the village Des Aulnats, employed by Mr. Dupuis, and he had charge of the fruit exhibit. Mr. Wil-mot, of the Geological Survey, had special qualifications for the setting up of the exhibits. He packed the geological exhibits and unpacked and set them up. Mr. Small went over to set up the honey and maple sugar exhibits. The honey had to be all taken and worked over before being exhibited. It was prepared a year before and was crystallized and not in fit condition to be exhibited. Anybody who understands the exhibiting of honey products knows that they have to be prepared immediately before being put on exhibition in warm weather. Mr. Small was an expert in bee culture, and he went to look after that exhibit. Mr. Angus R. Stuart, went from British Columbia practically as the representative of that province. He has been living there a good many years and is well known in connection with newspaper work there and was engaged somewhat in mining. He was recommended to me by my late colleague in the House, Mr. Bostock, as a gentleman well acquainted with the industry and resources of British Columbia. He was found very satisfactory, and I have appointed him to the Glasgow staff for the coming season.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: And as to Mrs. Turcotte ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Mrs. Turcotte is stenographer and typewriter, and went in that capacity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
There is an item in the Auditor General's Report, page D-14:
' Services and expenses re women's department, $1,749.41.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: That was largely expenses in connection with the preparation of the women's book, a publication prepared and compiled by a number of ladies well known in connection with the charitable and other work done by the Women's Council, and other women's work done in the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: So far as that work in Canada was concerned, it was entirely voluntary, was it not ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: There were some travelling expenses, printing, typewriting and editorial work. Allowances were also made to quite a number of the ladies who were not in a position, owing to financial circumstances, to devote their time to the work gratuitously. Much of the work was gratuitously done, and the general management was gratuitous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I am not finding fault with the gratuities to the ladies, but, speaking under correction, the work in my own province was done gratuitously.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I could not say who received gratuities or who did not. A good deal of the work was done by Miss Wilson, who is secretary to the Women's Council, and who acted aa editor and compiler. She was paid for her services.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: The hon. minister stated that the work done by Mr. Stuart was satisfactory. I am sorry to say that Mr. Stuart did not seem to think that the action of the hon. minister's colleague (the Minister of Public Works) was very satisfactory to him. I remember that a few months ago Mr. Stuart complained very bitterly about the treatment he received from the Minister of Public Works, stating to friends, and also to correspondents, that he had been behaved to most shabbily, and asked to do work derogatory to a man in his position. Does the hon. gentleman know of any complaints of Mr. Stuart, or was there any truth in the statements made to me ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I was just saying to my colleague that I never had more trouble with a staff than with this one in Paris. A good many of the employees, not all, but a certain number, seemed to think that they nad gone to Paris on a holiday.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: No, it is not correct; because there was a great deal of work to do. I do not wish to apply these remarks to Mr. Stuart. I do not remember treating him or any other employee in an improper way. I made them work as I worked myself. I know some of them did not like it, and I was obliged to send some of them home. I felt that Canada had a right to be represented by men who would keep sober and work, and would be on the spot when explanations were asked for.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: Mr. Stuart certainly made no complaint to me, when I saw him on his return ; he expressed himself as well pleased, and was extremely glad to get the appointment to go to Glasgow.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
I desire to ask the minister a question with reference to an article appearing in to-day's Montreall Gazette, which reads :
The Hon. Sidney Fisher, Minister of Agriculture, is having a unique map of the province of Quebec prepared for the Pan-American exposition. It will contain the physical features, forests, possible canoe trips, routes by the early missionaries, and by Champlain, and by other early French explorers, Hudson Bay forts, ancient Indian village sites, modern Indian reserves, regions of fish and game preserves-
-and so on. Is it the intention that Quebec shall be the only province mapped out in

that way for the Buffalo exposition, or may we expect that for the whole Dominion we shall have similar information furnished '!
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE, I have been requested, in connection with the ethnological exhibit at Buffalo, to assist to the extent of preparing a map for Quebec, as the Ontario government is preparing a map for that province in the same way. No arrangements have yet been made, and 1 have not given any orders in regard to the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext: I certainly think that what is done for one province ought to be done for another.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
speechtext:
Certainly.
Some resolutions reported.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-VISIT OF THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF CORNWALL AND YORK.

speechtext: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved the adjournment of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-VISIT OF THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF CORNWALL AND YORK.
speechtext:
I wish to draw the attention of the government to an item which appears in the government's organ, the Globe, of Toronto :
It is learned to-night from an official source that the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall have consented to go as far as Vancouver, but their trip west must necessarily be hurried, as their Royal Highnesses will he able to spend only a month in Canada.
The item says that their Highnesses will go as far as Vancouver. It is noticeable that the press all over this country, when speaking of British Columbia, always mention Vancouver as the most westerly city of the Dominion I wish to say that there is another city further west than Vancouver and of just as much importance, and more, for it is the capital of British Columbia and the seat of the greatest wealth by far of any city in the province. But it was not that point I rose to speak about. I desire to ask whether the government have any official information as to whether their Royal Highnesses had agreed to go to the Pacific coast or not, and whether they would go to Victoria.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-VISIT OF THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF CORNWALL AND YORK.
speechtext: I would prefer that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Prior) should put that question to-morrow, when the Prime Minister is in his place.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SOUTH AFRICAN WAR-PAY OF COLONIAL TROOPS.
subtopic: ADJOURNMENT-VISIT OF THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF CORNWALL AND YORK.
speechtext: I merely brought it up because it says it is from an official source.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Wednesday.
Wednesday, March 6, 1901.
